docs.title: How to Use This Book
docs.text:
• Read chapters in order — concepts are introduced in dependency order.
  • Use the search bar (top right) to jump to a specific term.
  • Try the MicroSims as you encounter them; they are the fastest way to build intuition for a new concept.
  • Check the Learning Graph when you want to see how a concept fits into the larger picture.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
This file is the seed document used by the learning-graph-generator skill to enumerate concepts, build the dependency graph, and assign concepts to a taxonomy. Keep it focused, concrete, and free of marketing language.

A good course description includes:

  • Title — same as site_name in mkdocs.yml
  • Audience — who this book is for and what they already know
  • Prerequisites — concepts the reader is assumed to have mastered
  • Topics — the major areas the book covers (typically 8–20 topics)
  • Bloom's Taxonomy outcomes — what the reader should be able to remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create by the end

Run the course-description-analyzer skill to validate completeness, then run learning-graph-generator to enumerate ~200 concepts with dependencies.

docs.title: Circuit Simulator Design
docs.text:
Status Design draft 1, for author review Date 2026-10-21 Implements Circuit Simulator Specification, draft 1 Focus of this pass Architectural components and the interfaces between them

The specification says what the simulator must do and deliberately says nothing about how. This document is the first answer to "how". It names the major components, draws the lines between them, defines the interfaces that cross those lines, and records why each significant option was chosen over its alternatives.

It is a first pass. Data structures inside a component, file-by-file code layout, and visual design are left for later passes. Where this document cites a requirement, the identifier (such as SIM-07) refers to the specification.

docs.title: 1. Pages in this design
docs.text: Page What it covers This page Goals, the overall architecture, threads, data flow, repository layout, and the summary of decisions Simulation Engine Numerical method, mixed-signal kernel, time stepping, the engine's command and output interfaces Circuit Model The circuit document, edits and undo, the netlist compiler, the element plug-in interface, subcircuits Rendering and Animation The schematic renderer, current dots, voltage color, and the time-series chart History and Analyses Time history, scrubbing, measurements, math traces, DC, frequency, sweep, and spectrum Application Shell UI framework, layout and responsiveness, tools and input, accessibility, settings Files and Persistence The circuit file, share links, Falstad import, browser storage, offline operation Embedding, Lessons, and xAPI Embed parameters and modes, the host message bridge, the lesson engine, learning events

docs.title: 2. Design goals
docs.text:
These goals come from the specification. When two design options both work, these settle the choice.

  1. The animation never stutters. The schematic and chart must stay smooth at 30–60 frames per second (PRF-01) and respond to a switch within 100 ms (PRF-02), even while the solver is working hard.
  2. The engine is testable without a browser. The 22 acceptance circuits (Section 26) and the 366 Falstad examples (FIL-18) must run as automated tests on every change, headless and fast.
  3. One source of truth per kind of state. The circuit document, the simulation state, and the user-interface state each have exactly one owner. Everything else is a view or a copy that can be rebuilt.
  4. Embeds are cheap. A chapter page may hold several embedded simulators. Each must show its circuit within two seconds (PRF-03), so code that a view or run embed never uses must not be loaded.
  5. Static hosting only. The book is published to GitHub Pages with mkdocs gh-deploy. There is no server, no custom HTTP headers, and no database. Everything runs in the reader's browser.
  6. Durable and open. Files are documented text, the app works offline, and nothing depends on a service that could close (PRN-12).

docs.title: 3. Architecture at a glance
docs.text:
The simulator is a single-page TypeScript application. It runs on two kinds of thread: the browser's main thread, which owns everything the reader sees and touches, and one or more web workers, which own the numerical work.

Click any component in the diagram to see its role, what it owns, what it connects to, and the requirements it serves. Press Next step to trace the slider edit described in §3.2 through the system. Dashed arrows cross between threads. Open the diagram full screen.

docs.title: 3.1 The components
docs.text: # Component Thread Owns Main requirements 1 Circuit Document Main Parts, wires, labels, probes, lanes, sliders, settings: everything saved in a file FIL-02, EDT-31 2 Edit and Undo System Main The undo and redo stacks; turns gestures into transactions EDT-31–33, PRN-05 3 Netlist Compiler Main Nothing persistent; turns geometry into nodes and a netlist CAN-10–12, EDT-14, EDT-39 4 Element Library Both One plug-in per part type: descriptor, model, view Section 9 5 Simulation Engine Worker Matrix, solver, element state, simulated time, the full-state history ring Section 10, Section 17, CHT-23 6 Engine Host Worker The run loop, speed control, frame batching SIM-01–11, PRF-09 7 Frame Bus Main Fan-out of each incoming frame to its subscribers PRN-04 8 History Store Main Probe traces at full resolution, ghosts, the event log CHT-17, CHT-24, PRF-04 9 Schematic Renderer Main Canvas layers, view transform, hit testing Section 6, Section 11 10 Current Animator Main Dot phases along every wire and part ANI-01–10 11 Chart Renderer Main Lanes, axes, traces, cursors, playhead Section 12 12 Measurement Library Main Pure functions over trace data CHT-26–33 13 Analysis Service Analysis worker DC, AC, sweep, spectrum jobs Section 14 14 Application Shell Main Layout, panels, menus, tools, focus, settings Sections 4, 5, 7, 8, 22, 24 15 Tool Controller Main The active tool and its state machine Sections 7, 8, 13 16 Persistence Service Main IndexedDB stores, autosave, recovery FIL-04–09, PRF-06 17 Format Codecs Main Native file, share link, Falstad text and XML FIL-01–03, FIL-14–19 18 Host Bridge Main Embed parameters, capabilities, host messages Section 19 19 Lesson Engine Main Lesson state, step progression, checks Section 20 20 xAPI Reporter Main Statement building, throttling, queue Section 21

docs.title: 3.2 How a change flows through the system
docs.text:
Following one edit end to end shows how the components fit together. The student drags a slider that changes R1 from 1 kΩ to 2 kΩ while the circuit runs:

  1. The Application Shell turns the slider drag into a gesture and hands it to the Edit and Undo System, which opens a transaction.
  2. Each pointer move updates the Circuit Document inside that open transaction. The document emits a patch: "R1.resistance = 1.37 kΩ".
  3. The Netlist Compiler classifies the patch. A value change does not alter topology, so no recompile is needed. It forwards a setParam command to the worker.
  4. The Engine Host applies the change before the next time step (SIM-18), adds an event marker (SIM-20), and keeps running.
  5. Within about 16 ms the worker posts a frame: new samples for every probe, the latest display state (node voltages and branch currents), and the event.
  6. The Frame Bus delivers the frame to the History Store (which appends it), the Schematic Renderer (wire colors), the Current Animator (dot speeds), the Chart Renderer (traces), and the Lesson Engine (checks).
  7. When the student releases the slider, the transaction closes as one undo step (EDT-32), the Persistence Service autosaves (PRF-06), and the xAPI Reporter sends one statement for the whole drag (XAP table, XAP-08).

A topology change (adding a part, rewiring) follows the same path, except that in step 3 the compiler produces a new netlist and the engine re-maps its state onto it by stable element identifiers, so that capacitors keep their charge (SIM-19). See Circuit Model §4.

docs.title: 3.3 Three kinds of state
docs.text:
State Owner Saved in file? Undoable? Examples Document Circuit Document Yes Yes Parts, values, wires, probes, lanes, sliders, circuit settings Simulation Engine (worker), mirrored by History Store Only part states at save time (FIL-17) No (EDT-33) Simulated time, node voltages, capacitor charge, logic states, failure status Session App Store No No Selection, zoom, active tool, open panels, chart cursors, learner settings

Keeping these three apart is the single most important structural rule in the design. It is what lets undo apply to a running circuit without rewinding time (EDT-33), lets the same document be shown in several embeds, and lets the engine run headless in tests.

Two exceptions that are deliberate

Failure state (RLM-07) is simulation state, but Repair is an undoable document edit that clears it. The view (zoom and center) is session state, but it is written into the file on save (FIL-02) and read back on open.

docs.title: 4.1 Where the simulation runs
docs.text:
The most consequential decision in this design is where the numerical work happens.

Option Description Verdict A. Main thread The solver runs between animation frames, as in Falstad's simulator. Rejected. A stiff circuit, a Newton iteration that needs many passes, or a 500-part matrix stalls the whole interface. PRF-02 and PRF-01 cannot be guaranteed. B. Dedicated worker, messages with transferable buffers The solver runs in a web worker. Each frame of results is packed into an ArrayBuffer and transferred (not copied) to the main thread. Chosen. C. Dedicated worker, SharedArrayBuffer ring buffers Worker and main thread share memory; no messages for data. Rejected for now. SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation (COOP and COEP headers). GitHub Pages cannot set headers, and an embedded iframe can only be isolated if the hosting chapter page is isolated too, which would break other content on the page.

Option B keeps the interface responsive no matter what the solver is doing, costs one small transfer per frame (a few kilobytes), and works on plain static hosting. The worker protocol is written so that option C can be added later behind the same interface if the book ever moves to a host that allows isolation.

docs.title: 4.2 The two clocks
docs.text:
Two clocks run independently, and keeping them separate is what makes ANI-03 true ("dot speed never depends on simulation speed"):

  • Simulated time advances in the worker. The Engine Host converts real elapsed time into a simulated-time budget using the speed setting (SIM-09), then steps the engine until the budget is used up or a frame deadline arrives.
  • Animation time advances on the main thread with requestAnimationFrame. The Current Animator moves dots using the latest known currents and real elapsed time. It never looks at the simulation speed.

If the worker cannot keep up, the Engine Host shrinks the budget rather than queueing work, and reports slowerThanRequested (PRF-09). The interface keeps animating at full frame rate with the most recent values.

docs.title: 4.3 Workers per page
docs.text: Each simulator instance (each iframe) has one live simulation worker, created at startup. An analysis worker is created only the first time an analysis tab is opened, and is shut down after a minute of idleness. A chapter page with four embeds therefore runs four live workers, which is acceptable because EMB-07 pauses embeds that are scrolled out of view.

docs.text: Area Chosen Main alternatives considered Why Language TypeScript (strict) everywhere Rust compiled to WebAssembly for the engine; C++ with Emscripten See §5.1 UI framework React 19 with React Aria Components Svelte 5; Lit web components See §5.2 Schematic drawing Canvas 2D, layered SVG; WebGL See Rendering §2.1 Chart drawing Custom Canvas 2D renderer uPlot; Plotly; a WebGL plot library See Rendering §5.1 Numerical method Modified nodal analysis, Newton–Raphson, trapezoidal with backward-Euler restarts, adaptive step Fixed-step backward Euler (Falstad); Gear/BDF2 See Engine §2 Digital logic Event-driven kernel coupled to the analog solver All gates as analog behavioral models See Engine §4 Undo Transactions of forward and inverse patches Command objects; full snapshots See Circuit Model §3 Circuit file Versioned JSON with a published JSON Schema YAML; a SPICE-like line format See Files §2 Lesson file YAML with a published JSON Schema Markdown with directives; JSON See Embedding §4.1 Browser storage IndexedDB (through a thin wrapper); localStorage only for learner settings Origin Private File System; localStorage for everything See Files §5 Build Vite, ES modules, code splitting Webpack; esbuild alone Fast development server, first-class workers, simple code splitting for embeds Tests Vitest (engine and model, run in Node), Playwright (user stories in real browsers) Jest; Cypress Vitest shares Vite's configuration; Playwright covers Chrome, Firefox, and Safari (PRF-08)

docs.title: 5.1 Why TypeScript for the engine, not WebAssembly
docs.text:
Option For Against TypeScript (chosen) One language for the whole project; the engine runs unchanged in Node for tests; easy to debug in browser tools; small download; modern JavaScript engines are fast enough for the matrix sizes this course needs (a 500-part circuit gives a sparse matrix of a few hundred to a thousand unknowns) Floating-point transcendental functions (Math.exp, Math.sin) are not guaranteed to give bit-identical results across browsers Rust to WebAssembly Fastest solver; bit-identical math everywhere Two languages and two toolchains; harder for textbook contributors; a crossing cost on every call between the engine and element models; larger download C++ with Emscripten (for example, wrapping ngspice) Professional-grade device models for free Very large download (several megabytes), poor fit for live editing and state re-mapping, and ngspice's license and batch-oriented design fight the "everything is live" principle

The engine is designed so that the hot inner kernel (sparse LU factorization and solve) sits behind a small interface, LinearSolver. If profiling on the reference laptop (open question 10) shows the solver is the bottleneck, that one kernel can be replaced with a WebAssembly build without touching anything else.

Determinism (PRN-09, SIM-23). Basic arithmetic in JavaScript is IEEE 754 and identical everywhere, but Math.exp, Math.log, Math.sin, and Math.pow may differ in the last bit between browsers. The engine therefore never calls them directly. It uses a small dmath module of deterministic implementations. Results are then identical in every supported browser, not only on repeated runs in one browser. Noise sources use a seeded generator (xoshiro128**) whose seed is stored in the file.

docs.title: 5.2 Why React with React Aria
docs.text:
The interface has many conventional pieces — menus, dialogs, the inspector's forms, the lesson panel, tables — and it must meet WCAG 2.2 AA (ACC-01). The hot paths (schematic, dots, chart) are drawn on canvases and do not go through the framework at all, so framework speed matters little. What matters is accessibility, responsive layout, and how many people can contribute.

Option For Against React 19 + React Aria Components (chosen) React Aria provides tested, accessible menus, dialogs, comboboxes, sliders, tabs, tables, and focus management, which covers most of Section 22; the largest pool of contributors and examples Larger runtime (about 45 kB compressed); needs care to keep frame-rate data out of React renders Svelte 5 Smaller output; fine-grained updates Its accessible-component libraries are younger; fewer contributors; we would hand-build more of ACC-02 to ACC-08 Lit web components Standards-based; tiny runtime; usable from any page No accessible component set of comparable depth; most WCAG work would be ours

The rule that keeps React fast here: frame-rate data never enters React state. Renderers subscribe to the Frame Bus directly. React components that show live numbers (hover cards, the legend's live values, the multimeter) subscribe through a hook that samples the bus at most ten times a second.

docs.title: 6. Code organization
docs.text:
The application lives in a new top-level app/ folder, separate from the MkDocs content in docs/. It is a single npm workspace with packages whose dependencies point one way only, so the engine can never accidentally depend on the interface:

app/
  packages/
    units/         number parsing and formatting (EDT-26), unit algebra (CHT-33)
    dmath/         deterministic math functions and seeded random numbers
    model/         circuit document, patches, undo, netlist compiler   -> units
    elements/      one folder per part type: descriptor, model, view   -> model, units
    engine/        solver, integrator, digital kernel, analyses        -> elements (models only), dmath
    worker/        engine host and run loop; worker entry points       -> engine
    formats/       native file, share link, Falstad codecs             -> model, elements
    render/        schematic renderer, animator, chart renderer        -> model, elements (views only)
    lesson/        lesson schema, loader, checks, step machine         -> model
    xapi/          statement builder, queue                            -> (none)
    app/           React shell, stores, tools, host bridge, persistence -> everything
  tests/
    acceptance/    the 22 circuits of Section 26, run headless in Node
    library/       opens all 366 Falstad examples (test 20)
    stories/       Playwright walk-throughs of the Section 25 user stories

Dependency rule. engine and everything it depends on must run in Node with no DOM. A lint rule enforces it. This is what makes design goal 2 possible.

docs.title: 6.1 Where the built app lives on the site
docs.text:
vite build writes the finished simulator into docs/simulator/, so that mkdocs build copies it into the site and the book can link to https://dmccreary.github.io/circuit-simulator/simulator/?example=lrc.txt (FIL-19). Embeds in chapters are then same-origin with the book, which simplifies the host bridge's origin check (EMB-12) and lets the browser share one cached copy of the simulator across every chapter.

Whether docs/simulator/ is committed or built just before each publish is an open question for the author (§8, question 1).

docs.title: 7.1 Errors and diagnostics
docs.text:
Every component reports problems as structured diagnostics, never as bare strings, so that the interface can highlight parts and offer fixes (PRN-06, EDT-39, SIM-14):

interface Diagnostic {
  id: string;                 // stable kind, such as "sources-in-parallel"
  severity: "info" | "warning" | "error";
  message: MessageRef;        // a translation key plus values, never English text
  elements: ElementId[];      // parts and wires to highlight
  nodes?: NodeId[];
  fixes?: FixAction[];        // each fix is a document transaction the user can apply
  simTime?: number;           // for solver errors (SIM-16)
}

The netlist compiler produces structural diagnostics (no ground, floating sections, sources in parallel). The engine produces numerical ones (singular matrix, failure to converge), which it maps back to the parts involved by inspecting the matrix row or column that failed. Lessons attach their own feedback to diagnostics by id (LES-11).

docs.title: 7.2 Internationalization
docs.text: All interface and diagnostic text goes through message keys and ICU message formatting. Number formatting with units (EDT-26) is in the units package and is locale-aware for the decimal separator, while unit symbols and metric prefixes stay in SI form in every language.

docs.title: 7.3 Theming
docs.text: Colors are design tokens defined once per theme (light, dark, high contrast). Canvas renderers read the same tokens as the CSS, so the schematic, chart, and panels always agree (CAN-15). Voltage color scales and the probe palette are token sets with a separate set per theme, chosen for contrast and color-blind safety (ACC-11, ACC-12).

docs.title: 7.4 Testing strategy
docs.text: Layer What is tested How units, dmath, model, formats Parsing, patches, undo, netlist compilation, round-trip of files Vitest unit tests in Node engine Every acceptance circuit in Section 26 with its tolerance; determinism (same input, bit-identical output) Vitest in Node; a golden-file test per circuit Library All 366 Falstad examples open; 20 author-chosen examples match Falstad's waveforms within 1% (test 21) Vitest in Node, using reference waveforms captured once from Falstad's simulator Rendering Visual regression of the schematic and chart Playwright screenshots Whole app Each user story in Section 25, as written Playwright in Chrome, Firefox, and WebKit Performance 150-part circuit at 30 fps or better (test 22) Playwright with a trace, on the reference laptop Accessibility WCAG 2.2 AA rules axe-core in Playwright, plus manual screen-reader passes

docs.title: 8. Open questions for the author
docs.text:
1. Committing the build. Should docs/simulator/ (the built app) be committed so that the existing "publish" routine (commit, push, mkdocs gh-deploy) always ships the latest simulator, or should it be ignored by git and built by a script just before publishing? Recommendation: ignore it in git and add one npm run build step to the publish routine, so the repository does not fill up with build output.
  2. Reference laptop. Specification question 10 matters directly here: it decides whether the TypeScript solver is fast enough or whether the WebAssembly kernel (§5.1) is needed for the first release.
  3. License. Specification question 2 decides which third-party code the engine may borrow (for example, device model equations from GPL-licensed sources).

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: This design builds on the Circuit Simulator Specification, which in turn draws on Paul Falstad's CircuitJS1 and the other sources listed in its Sources section. Specific ideas borrowed from other projects are credited on the page where they are used.

docs.title: Application Shell
docs.text: The application shell is everything the student touches that is not a canvas: the top bar, palette, inspector, chart panel chrome, menus, dialogs, lesson panel, and status bar. It also hosts the tool controller, which interprets pointer and keyboard input on the canvas. It is built with React and React Aria Components (Overview §5.2).

docs.title: 1. Stores
docs.text:
The shell reads from three stores, matching the three kinds of state in the overview:

Store Holds Updated by Read by React? Document store The current CircuitDocument The Edit System only Yes, with selectors so a component re-renders only when its slice changes App store Session state: selection, active tool, open panels, layout, chart cursors, run state, diagnostics, capabilities, learner settings Shell actions; worker run-state messages Yes Live values The latest frame The Frame Bus, up to 60 times a second Only through useLiveValue(channel), which samples at most 10 times a second

The third row is the performance rule from the overview in practice: a hover card or the legend shows live numbers without the whole tree re-rendering every frame.

docs.title: 2. The command registry
docs.text:
Every action the student can take — Run, Undo, Rotate, Add slider, Plot voltage, Open, Fit — is registered once as a command:

interface Command {
  id: CommandId;                         // "sim.run", "edit.rotateCW", "probe.plotVoltage"
  label: MessageRef;
  icon?: IconName;
  defaultKeys?: KeyChord[];              // Section 8
  when?: (ctx: CommandContext) => boolean;      // visible and enabled
  capability?: Capability;               // required permission (§6)
  run(ctx: CommandContext, args?: unknown): void | Promise<void>;
}
Option Verdict Each menu, toolbar, and shortcut wires its own handler Rejected: shortcuts drift from menus, remapping (SET-06) has nothing to remap, and lessons cannot hide features in one place. A central command registry Chosen.

The registry is then the one place that feeds:

  • the menus, toolbars, and context menus (built from command lists);
  • the keyboard map, remappable with conflict detection (SET-06), and the ? shortcut list generated from it (Section 8);
  • permissions: a command whose capability is not granted by the embed mode or lesson is hidden (§6);
  • the xAPI reporter, which listens for executed commands it reports (Section 21);
  • lesson spotlights, which can point at any command's control by id (LES-09).

docs.title: 3.1 Choosing a layout
docs.text:
The shell measures its own root element with a ResizeObserver and derives a width class (extra wide, wide, medium, narrow) and a height class (normal or short, below 520 px) from Section 5. It does not use the device's screen size, so an iframe in a narrow column of a chapter page gets the narrow layout even on a large monitor (Section 5, first paragraph).

type Layout = {
  width: "xwide" | "wide" | "medium" | "narrow";
  height: "normal" | "short";
  pointer: "fine" | "coarse";            // from the pointer media query (RSP-13)
  arrangement: "side" | "stacked" | "single";
  narrowView?: "circuit" | "chart" | "both";   // the Narrow segmented switch
};
Class Arrangement Palette Inspector Dialogs Extra wide Side by side, 60/40 Labelled list Docked below the canvas Centered Wide Side by side Icon rail with fly-outs Docked Centered Medium Stacked, 60/40 by height Icon rail Bottom sheet Bottom sheet Narrow One view at a time, or Both Full-height drawer Bottom sheet Full screen Short (any width) As above, compact top bar — Pop-over —

docs.title: 3.2 Keeping state across layouts
docs.text: RSP-02 says changing class must lose nothing. The design guarantees it structurally: no component keeps important state of its own. The selection, zoom and pan, chart cursors, panel sizes, and run state all live in the stores, so a panel can be unmounted in one layout and remounted in another without losing anything. The canvases are not recreated when the layout changes; they are moved and resized.

docs.title: 3.3 Panels and splitters
docs.text: The main area is a small tree of split panes (schematic and chart, then schematic and inspector). Splitters are React Aria focusable separators with arrow-key movement (LAY-09), double-click reset to 60/40, minimum sizes (LAY-10), and collapse to a labelled tab (LAY-12). Layout sizes are remembered per browser (LAY-11).

docs.title: 4. The main panels
docs.text: Panel Built from Notes Top bar Commands Run/Pause, Step, Reset, time readout (SIM-05), speed control with ratio in words (SIM-09), realism badge (RLM-03), lesson progress (LAY-01) Palette Element descriptors Categories in CMP-01 order, Essentials-first (CMP-02), search over names and aliases (EDT-03), filtered by capabilities Inspector Element descriptors' PropSpec lists One generated form for every part type; number fields use the units parser (EDT-26) and refuse out-of-range values with the range (EDT-27); several parts of one kind show "mixed" (EDT-29) Chart panel chrome Document lanes, chart model Legend chips, lane titles, analysis tabs (ANL-01), measurement table; the plot areas are canvases (Rendering §5) Slider panel Document sliders CTL-05 Status bar App store Run state with icon (SIM-06), warning count opening the diagnostics list, hover readout (LAY-06), slower-than-requested notice (PRF-09), recording indicator (XAP-03) Lesson panel Lesson engine Embedding §4

docs.title: 5.1 The tool controller
docs.text:
Canvas input is handled by a tool controller that holds exactly one active tool. Each tool is a small state machine:

interface Tool {
  id: ToolId;                 // "select", "place", "wire", "probe-v", "probe-i", "probe-p",
                              // "loop", "junction", "annotate", "pan"
  cursor(ctx: ToolContext): CursorShape;            // PRB-05: probe tip, clamp, thermometer
  onPointerDown?(e: CanvasPointer, ctx: ToolContext): void;
  onPointerMove?(e: CanvasPointer, ctx: ToolContext): void;
  onPointerUp?(e: CanvasPointer, ctx: ToolContext): void;
  onKey?(e: KeyChord, ctx: ToolContext): boolean;   // true if handled
  drawOverlay?(g: OverlayGraphics, ctx: ToolContext): void;   // previews (PRB-04, EDT-05, EDT-06)
  cancel?(ctx: ToolContext): void;                   // Esc
}

ToolContext gives a tool everything it may use and nothing else: hit testing on the compiled circuit, the edit system (to open transactions), the live values (for previews such as PRB-04), the app store, and the view transform. Tools never touch the engine directly; everything they change goes through document edits or control commands.

docs.title: 5.2 Input normalization
docs.text:
All input arrives as Pointer Events, so mouse, pen, and touch share one path. A gesture layer in front of the tools recognizes:

  • two-finger pan and pinch zoom (RSP-14);
  • tap-and-hold, which shows the hover card for touch (RSP-15);
  • middle-drag and Space-drag panning (CAN-04);
  • wheel behavior that depends on embedding: zoom in the full app, scroll the page in an embed unless Ctrl is held or the simulator has been clicked (EMB-05).

docs.title: 5.3 Controls while running
docs.text: Switches, push buttons, potentiometer wipers, and logic inputs are operated in the Select tool by clicking their control regions (provided by each element view). Operating a control is not a selection (CTL-01). A push button holds while the pointer or Space is held (CTL-02). Control changes go through the edit system like any other value change, so the engine, undo, xAPI, and lesson checks all see them in the same way.

docs.title: 5.4 Keyboard operation of the canvas
docs.text:
Keyboard-only editing (ACC-02–05) is a focus cursor on the canvas, separate from the selection (ACC-03):

  • Tab and Shift+Tab move between parts in reading order; Alt+arrow moves to the connected neighbor in that direction.
  • [ and ] cycle the focused part's terminals; W starts a wire from the focused terminal; arrows then jump between candidate terminals and wire ends; Enter connects (ACC-04).
  • Placing from the palette or quick-add with Enter drops the part at the view center, selected, ready to move with the arrows (ACC-05).

Every one of these is a command in the registry, so they are remappable and appear in the shortcut list.

docs.title: 6. Capabilities
docs.text:
Embed modes (EMB-02), lesson permissions (LES-01), locked parts, and the learner's own choices all reduce to one capability set held in the app store:

interface Capabilities {
  edit: "full" | "values" | "none";      // edit, run, view modes
  palette: "all" | string[];             // allowed part types (CMP-02, LES-01)
  tools: ToolId[];
  panels: PanelId[];                     // embed `panels` parameter
  analyses: AnalysisKind[] | "none";
  chartVisible: boolean;
  lockedParts: Id[];                     // EMB `lock`, lessons
  hidden?: { readouts: boolean; traces: boolean; animation: boolean };   // LES-03 blind prediction
}

The capability set is the only thing the shell consults to decide what to show. Commands, tools, palette entries, and panels each check it. Embed parameters and lessons merely compute a capability set; neither reaches into the interface directly.

docs.title: 7. Accessibility
docs.text:
Section 22 is a constraint on every component, but four pieces belong to the shell:

Piece Design The accessible circuit tree (ACC-06, ACC-07) The canvas is paired with a visually hidden, structured DOM list of parts, wires, nodes, and probes, generated from the compiled circuit. Each item's accessible name comes from its element view's describe, with live values from the live-values store. The canvas focus cursor and this list are kept in step, so a screen reader announces the focused part. Announcer (ACC-08) One polite live region with a rate limit of one announcement per kind of event every two seconds; diagnostics, failures, lesson feedback, and check results all go through it. Chart alternatives (ACC-09) A data table view and generated text descriptions of each trace, built from the History Store and the measurement library. Sonification (ACC-10) A Web Audio oscillator whose pitch follows the selected trace, sharing the audio path with speakers (ANI-20).

React Aria provides keyboard behavior, focus management, and ARIA roles for menus, dialogs, tabs, sliders, tables, and the color and number fields, which covers most of the remaining WCAG 2.2 AA work (ACC-01).

docs.title: 8. Settings
docs.text:
Settings resolve in layers, each overriding the one before:

built-in defaults  <  learner settings (browser)  <  embed parameters  <  lesson
  • Learner settings (SET-01) are a small, versioned JSON object in localStorage, read synchronously at startup so the first frame already has the right theme and symbol style. They are never written into circuit files (SET-04).
  • Circuit settings (SET-02) live in the document and are undoable.
  • Embed parameters may override a learner setting for one embed only (SET-04) and are never saved back.
  • Interface scale (SET-03) sets the root font size, which every panel size is expressed in, and multiplies the canvases' device-pixel ratio so the schematic and chart stay sharp.

docs.title: Circuit Model
docs.text: The circuit model is the single source of truth for everything the student builds. It lives on the main thread and contains no physics. The engine never sees it directly: the netlist compiler translates it into the netlist the engine solves.

docs.title: 1. Responsibilities
docs.text: Component Responsibility Circuit Document Holds every saved thing: parts, wires, net labels, annotations, probes, chart lanes, sliders, scheduled actions, subcircuit definitions, circuit settings, title, and description (FIL-02) Edit and Undo System Turns gestures into transactions, keeps the undo and redo stacks, and broadcasts patches (EDT-31–33) Netlist Compiler Works out which points are connected, names the nodes, flattens subcircuits, checks the circuit, and produces the netlist (CAN-10–12, EDT-14, EDT-39) Element Registry Holds one plug-in per part type and loads rarely used ones on demand (Section 9)

docs.title: 2.1 Entities
docs.text:
The document is a normalized collection of entities, each with a stable identifier that never changes and is never shown to the student. The student-visible label (R1, V2) is an ordinary property that can be renamed. Keeping the two apart is what lets probes, sliders, lesson checks, and the engine's state re-mapping survive renaming and rewiring.

type Id = string;                 // short random identifier, unique in the document

interface CircuitDocument {
  formatVersion: number;
  meta: { title: string; description: string };      // FIL-10
  settings: CircuitSettings;                          // SET-02
  parts: Record<Id, Part>;
  wires: Record<Id, Wire>;
  netLabels: Record<Id, NetLabel>;                    // EDT-14; ground is a net label "GND"
  annotations: Record<Id, Annotation>;                // CAN-13
  probes: Record<Id, Probe>;                          // Section 13
  lanes: Lane[];                                      // CHT-01–04, in display order
  mathTraces: Record<Id, MathTrace>;                  // CHT-33
  sliders: Record<Id, Slider>;                        // CTL-05
  subcircuits: Record<Id, SubcircuitDefinition>;      // EDT-34–38
  analyses: AnalysisSettings;                         // ANL settings saved with the file
  view: { center: Point; zoom: number };              // FIL-02
}

interface Part {
  id: Id;
  type: string;                    // element type, such as "resistor" or "falstad:placeholder"
  label: string;                   // "R1"
  at: Point;                       // grid coordinates of the first terminal
  orientation: Orientation;        // rotation and flip (EDT-02, EDT-21)
  length?: number;                 // two-terminal parts, in grid units (EDT-07)
  props: Record<string, PropValue>;// values as numbers in SI units, plus enums and text
  labelOffset?: Point;             // student-dragged label (CAN-08)
  locked?: boolean;                // EMB `lock`, lessons
  savedState?: number[];           // capacitor voltage and the like, written on save
}

interface Wire {
  id: Id;
  points: Point[];                 // grid points; right-angled segments (EDT-09, EDT-10)
}

All geometry is in integer grid units (CAN-02). Pixels appear only in the renderer. Falstad's 16-pixel grid maps to one unit on import (FIL-17).

docs.title: 2.2 Probes refer to places, not nodes
docs.text:
A node is not a stable thing: joining two wires merges two nodes, and deleting a wire can split one. A probe therefore never stores a node name. It stores the place the student clicked, and the compiler resolves the place to a node every time it runs:

type ProbeTarget =
  | { kind: "point"; wire: Id; segment: number; t: number }    // a spot on a wire
  | { kind: "terminal"; part: Id; terminal: number }
  | { kind: "across"; part: Id }                               // voltage across a part
  | { kind: "between"; a: ProbeTarget; b: ProbeTarget }        // differential (red, black)
  | { kind: "through"; part: Id; terminal?: number; reversed: boolean } // PRB-06, PRB-07
  | { kind: "segment"; wire: Id; segment: number; reversed: boolean };

interface Probe {
  id: Id;
  name: string;                    // "V1", renameable (CHT-06)
  quantity: "voltage" | "current" | "power" | "logic";
  target: ProbeTarget;
  style: TraceStyle;               // color, width, dash, marker (CHT-15)
  lane: Id;
  flag: { offset: Point; showValue: boolean };   // PRB-09, PRB-10
  measurements: MeasurementSpec[]; // CHT-30
}

If the thing a target refers to is deleted, the probe is removed in the same transaction and the student sees "Probe I2 removed with R3" with Undo (PRB-12).

docs.title: 3.1 Options considered
docs.text:
Option Description Verdict A. Command objects Each action is a class with do() and undo(). Rejected. Every one of the hundreds of editing actions needs hand-written, hand-tested undo code, and bugs in it silently corrupt circuits. B. Full snapshots Save a copy of the whole document before each change. Rejected. Simple and safe, but costly for large circuits with no undo limit (EDT-31), and it says nothing about what changed, which the netlist compiler, autosave, and xAPI reporter all need. C. Transactions of patches Every change is expressed as small patches ("set parts.R7.props.resistance to 2200"). The system records each patch with its inverse. Chosen.

Patches give undo for free (apply the inverses in reverse order), and the same patch stream tells every other component exactly what changed:

  • the netlist compiler decides whether a recompile is needed;
  • the persistence service autosaves (PRF-06);
  • the xAPI reporter describes the change (Section 21);
  • the lesson engine re-evaluates only the checks the patch affects (LES-08).

The document is stored as plain immutable objects with structural sharing, so a patch replaces only the objects along its path. React components and renderers can detect changes by identity comparison.

docs.title: 3.2 Transactions and gestures
docs.text:
interface EditSystem {
  /** Start a gesture. Edits made until commit or cancel become one undo step (EDT-32). */
  begin(label: MessageRef, options?: { coalesceKey?: string }): Transaction;
  undo(): void;
  redo(): void;
  canUndo: boolean;
  canRedo: boolean;
  onPatches(listener: (p: PatchBatch) => void): Unsubscribe;
}

interface Transaction {
  update(recipe: (draft: CircuitDocument) => void): void;   // may be called many times
  commit(): void;
  cancel(): void;                                           // reverts every update
}
  • One gesture, one step. A drag, a whole slider movement, or a paste is one transaction, however many updates it makes along the way. The patches inside an open transaction still flow to the engine as they happen, so the circuit responds continuously (CTL-06), but the undo stack records only the net change on commit.
  • Normalization runs inside the transaction. Merging straight wire runs, removing zero-length wires (EDT-13), splitting a wire when a part is dropped onto it (EDT-06), and assigning the next free label (EDT-08) happen in a normalize pass before commit, so the undo step includes them.
  • Undo never touches time. Undoing sends the inverse patches through the same path as any other edit. The engine applies them live (EDT-33); running, pausing, and the passage of time are never recorded.
  • Lesson snapshots. Reset Step (LES-12) and Reset to original (EMB-04) restore a saved document snapshot as one transaction, which is itself undoable.

docs.title: 4. The netlist compiler
docs.text:
The compiler is a pure function from document to netlist, run whenever a patch could change connectivity. It runs on the main thread because it needs the document and the element views' terminal positions, and because its diagnostics are shown immediately on the canvas.

interface NetlistCompiler {
  compile(doc: CircuitDocument, previous?: CompiledCircuit): CompiledCircuit;
  classify(patches: PatchBatch): "none" | "params" | "topology";
}

interface CompiledCircuit {
  netlist: Netlist;                  // what the engine receives
  nodes: NodeTable;                  // node id, display name, member points, digital or analog
  pointToNode: SpatialIndex<NodeId>; // for hover (CAN-11) and probe placement
  segments: SegmentTable;            // every drawn wire segment and part path, for dots
  channels: ChannelTable;            // probe targets resolved to engine channels
  identity: IdentityMap;             // old element ids to new, for state re-mapping (SIM-19)
  diagnostics: Diagnostic[];         // structural checks (EDT-39)
}

docs.title: 4.1 Stages
docs.text:
1. Collect connection points. Every terminal position, every wire end, and every wire bend becomes a point. A terminal or wire end that lands on the middle of another wire splits that wire there (EDT-11). Crossing wires without a shared point do not connect (CAN-10).
  2. Union the points into nodes with a disjoint-set structure: points joined by a wire segment, points at the same grid location, and all net labels with the same name (EDT-14). Ground symbols are net labels named GND (CAN-12).
  3. Name the nodes. Labelled nets take their label. Others get N1, N2, …, chosen so the same node keeps the same name across edits: each node's name is anchored to the oldest terminal it contains and is reused while that terminal stays on it. Names that jump around would make probe legends and lesson text confusing.
  4. Flatten subcircuits (§6).
  5. Classify each node as analog, digital, or mixed (digital bridges, Engine §4).
  6. Check the circuit and produce diagnostics: no ground, floating sections, dangling ends, sources in parallel, an ideal current source with no path, shorts across sources, overlapping parts, ammeters in parallel, voltmeters in series (EDT-39), and Falstad placeholders (FIL-16). Most checks are graph searches on the node graph (for example, a loop of voltage sources and wires is a cycle that contains no other element).
  7. Resolve channels. Every probe, meter, tool, lesson check, and pause condition target is resolved to an engine channel (a node pair, a branch, or a segment).
  8. Build the identity map from the previous compilation, so the engine can carry state across (SIM-19).

docs.title: 4.2 Incremental work
docs.text: Recompiling a 500-part circuit takes a few milliseconds, which is fast enough to recompile on every topology change without optimization. What matters more is not recompiling when nothing structural changed: classify sends value changes (the common case while dragging a slider) straight to the engine as setParams without running stages 1–8.

docs.title: 5. The element plug-in interface
docs.text:
Each part type in Section 9 is a folder in the elements package with three parts, split so that the worker never loads drawing code and the interface never loads physics code:

elements/resistor/
  descriptor.ts   pure data, loaded everywhere
  model.ts        ElementModel, loaded only in workers
  view.ts         ElementView, loaded only on the main thread
  help.md         the help card (CMP-08)

docs.title: 5.1 The descriptor
docs.text:
interface ElementDescriptor {
  type: string;                      // "resistor"
  category: CategoryId;              // CMP-01
  essentials?: boolean;              // shown to new learners (CMP-02)
  aliases: string[];                 // quick-add search (EDT-03): "res", "ohm"
  hotkey?: string;                   // EDT-04
  labelPrefix: string;               // "R" (EDT-08)
  terminals: TerminalSpec[];         // names, positions in the symbol frame, first-terminal mark (CMP-05)
  stretchable?: { min: number; default: number };   // EDT-07
  props: PropSpec[];                 // see below
  models?: NamedModel[];             // CMP-07: "1N4148", "LM741", plus Custom
  ratings?: RatingSpec[];            // RLM-04
  readouts: ReadoutSpec[];           // what the hover card shows (CAN-17)
  falstad?: FalstadMapping;          // how to import and export (FIL-17)
}

interface PropSpec {
  key: string;                       // "resistance"
  unit: Unit;                        // "ohm"; drives parsing (EDT-26) and display
  range: [number, number];           // EDT-27, CMP-06
  default: PropValue;
  realisticDefault?: PropValue;      // used when Realistic parts is on (RLM-01)
  sliderable?: boolean;              // EDT-30
  standardSeries?: boolean;          // EDT-28
  showOnCanvas?: boolean;            // the main value next to the symbol (CAN-08)
}

The descriptor alone is enough to build the palette, the quick-add search, the inspector's form, the Falstad importer, and the help card. Most of the user interface for a new part therefore comes for free.

docs.title: 5.2 The model
docs.text: The engine half, defined in Simulation Engine §5.

docs.title: 5.3 The view
docs.text:
interface ElementView {
  /** Draw the symbol in its local frame. Called rarely; the result is cached. */
  drawSymbol(g: SymbolGraphics, part: Part, style: "ansi" | "iec" | "lifelike"): void;

  /** Draw state that changes while running: glow, charge marks, wiper, contacts. */
  drawLive?(g: LiveGraphics, part: Part, live: LiveReadouts): void;

  /** The paths current takes through the part, for the dots (ANI-01). */
  currentPaths(part: Part): Polyline[];

  /** Regions that react to clicks while running: a switch lever, a pot wiper (CTL-01–04). */
  controls?(part: Part): ControlRegion[];

  /** Hit area for selection and hover, slightly larger on touch (RSP-13). */
  hitShape(part: Part): Shape;

  /** Accessible description (ACC-07). */
  describe(part: Part, live?: LiveReadouts): MessageRef;
}

docs.title: 5.4 The registry and lazy loading
docs.text: The registry maps type names to plug-ins. The Essentials parts are bundled with the application. Every other category is a separate code chunk loaded the first time a circuit or the palette needs it. A chapter embed of an RC circuit therefore never downloads the 74181 arithmetic logic unit (design goal 4).

docs.title: 6. Subcircuits
docs.text:
A subcircuit definition is a small circuit document of its own (parts and wires) plus a list of pins, each tied to a node inside and placed on the edge of the block symbol (EDT-34). Definitions are stored in the document (subcircuits), so a file is self-contained, and are also kept in browser storage for the My parts palette (EDT-35).

  • Instances are ordinary parts of type subcircuit whose props name the definition.
  • Flattening. The compiler copies each instance's contents into the netlist with hierarchical identifiers (U1/R3, U1/N2), connecting pins to the outer nodes. The engine never sees hierarchy.
  • Looking inside (EDT-36) opens a nested view of the same definition. Probes placed inside store a path (U1/…) in their target, so their traces appear on the main chart.
  • Black boxes (EDT-37) set a sealed flag on the definition. A sealed definition cannot be opened, and its hover card shows only pin values.
  • Built-in subcircuits such as the 555 timer's inside view are definitions shipped with the element library and marked read-only.
  • Editing one copy or all (EDT-38) is a document operation: "all" edits the definition; "this one" copies the definition under a new identifier and repoints the instance, both in one transaction.

docs.title: 7. Open questions
docs.text: 1. Sharing subcircuits between circuits. If a student edits a My parts definition, should circuits that already contain an older copy be offered the update? This design keeps each file's copy unchanged unless the student asks, which is safer but can leave several versions with one name.

docs.title: Embedding, Lessons, and xAPI
docs.text: These three features connect the simulator to the textbook around it. They are designed together because they share two mechanisms: the capability set that decides what the reader may do (Application Shell §6), and the host bridge that carries messages between the simulator and the chapter page.

docs.title: 1. Components
docs.text: Component Responsibility Embed loader Reads the URL parameters, chooses what code to load, computes the starting capability set (Section 19.1–19.2) Host bridge The postMessage channel to the page that embeds the simulator (Section 19.4) Host helper script A small script that chapter pages include to size iframes and relay messages (EMB-08, XAP-01) Lesson engine Loads lesson files, runs the step machine, evaluates checks, stores predictions and progress (Section 20) xAPI reporter Turns learner actions into xAPI statements, throttles them, queues them, and sends them (Section 21)

docs.title: 2.1 Start-up for an embed
docs.text:
PRF-03 gives an embed two seconds to show its circuit, and a chapter may hold several. The embed start-up is ordered to show something useful as early as possible:

  1. Parse the parameters into an EmbedConfig. Unknown parameters are ignored; invalid values fall back to their defaults and add a warning (EMB-01).
  2. Load only what the mode needs. view and run embeds load a smaller entry bundle without the palette, the wiring tools, the inspector's editors, subcircuit editing, or the lesson author tools. edit mode and the full simulator load everything. Element plug-ins load by category on demand (Circuit Model §5.4).
  3. Fetch and decode the circuit (from circuit, example, ctz, or c).
  4. Draw the schematic at once, before the worker is ready, using the document alone (no voltage colors yet).
  5. Start the worker, load the netlist, and compute the t = 0 solution. The circuit stays paused (SIM-01a); colors and readouts appear.
  6. Post ready and the preferred height to the host.

docs.title: 2.2 Modes become capabilities
docs.text:
Each mode (EMB-02) is a preset capability set; the panels, lock, and layout parameters then narrow it:

Mode edit Tools Notes edit "full" All The full simulator run "values" Select, probes, Loop, Junction Values of unlocked parts can change; no adding, deleting, or rewiring view "none" Select (hover only), pause, scrub No changes at all lesson From the lesson file From the lesson file Recomputed at each step (§4.2)

Recommended chapter default. Most chapter embeds should use mode=run&panels=chart,status. This hides the palette, inspector, and top-bar editing menus, keeps Run/Pause, switches, sliders, probes, and the chart, and keeps the reader's attention on the circuit the text is discussing. The Open in full simulator control that every embed shows (EMB-03) is the reader's way into full editing.

docs.title: 2.3 Embed controls
docs.text:
• Open in full simulator (EMB-03) encodes the current document, including the reader's changes, as a share link (Files §3) and opens it in a new tab in edit mode.
  • Reset to original (EMB-04) re-loads the document as published, as one undoable transaction, and clears the reader's saved changes for this embed.

docs.title: 2.4 The host helper script and markup
docs.text:
Chapter authors embed a simulator with an ordinary iframe plus one script include:

<iframe class="circuit-sim"
        src="../../simulator/?example=lrc.txt&mode=run&panels=chart,status&id=ch3-lrc"
        title="Series LRC circuit simulation"
        width="100%" height="480"></iframe>
<script src="../../simulator/embed.js"></script>

embed.js (a few kilobytes, no dependencies) finds every iframe.circuit-sim on the page, listens for preferredHeight messages and resizes each iframe so it has no inner scrollbar (EMB-08), and, when the page has configured xAPI, relays statements to the page's learning record store connection. Without the script, embeds still work at the iframe's given height (EMB-08, last sentence).

docs.title: 3.1 Message envelope
docs.text:
Every message, in both directions, uses one envelope:

interface BridgeMessage<T extends string, P> {
  protocol: "circuit-simulator";
  version: 1;
  embedId: string;          // the `id` parameter, so a page with many embeds can tell them apart
  type: T;                  // "ready", "loadCircuit", "setValue", ...
  requestId?: string;       // set on requests that expect a reply, such as getState
  payload: P;
}
Direction Types (EMB-10, EMB-11) Simulator to host ready, preferredHeight, runStateChanged, circuitChanged, lessonProgress, xapiStatement, reply Host to simulator loadCircuit, setValue, setSwitch, run, pause, reset, addProbe, configureXapi, getState

docs.title: 3.2 Trust rules (EMB-12)
docs.text:
• A message is accepted only if its source is the simulator's own parent window and its origin equals the parent's origin, which the bridge records at start-up (from location.ancestorOrigins where the browser provides it, otherwise from document.referrer).
  • The envelope and payload are validated against a schema. Anything malformed is ignored without error.
  • Host commands go through the command registry and the capability set like any reader action: a host cannot make a view embed edit its circuit. setValue may target any part's property, or a host input part (Section 9.3), which is how a page drives a circuit from its own controls.
  • Outgoing messages are posted to the recorded parent origin, never to "*", so circuit data never leaks to an unexpected page.

docs.title: 4.1 The lesson file
docs.text:
Option For Against Verdict YAML with a published JSON Schema Pleasant to write by hand; comments allowed; teachers can copy a step and edit it; the schema gives editor autocompletion and validation (LES-16) Parser size (loaded only in lesson mode); YAML's implicit typing, which the schema catches Chosen Markdown with directive blocks Feels like the textbook's own pages Step structure, checks, and permissions are data, not prose; hard to validate reliably Rejected JSON Same format as circuits No comments; unpleasant to write by hand Rejected

A short example:

lesson: current-is-not-used-up
title: Is current used up by a bulb?
time: 10 min
objectives: [Predict and measure current on both sides of a lamp]
concepts: [Electric Current, Series Circuit]          # learning-graph concept names
circuit: circuits/one-lamp.circuit.json
permissions:
  palette: [ammeter]
  tools: [select, probe-i]
  locked: [V1, L1]
steps:
  - read: "A 9 V battery lights one lamp. We will compare the current before and after the lamp."
    spotlight: [L1]
  - predict-choice:
      prompt: "Compared with the current entering L1, the current leaving it is..."
      options: [larger, the same, smaller]
      blind: [readouts, animation]                     # LES-03
  - do:
      prompt: "Place a current probe on each side of L1."
      check:
        all:
          - probe: { quantity: current, on: wire, touching: L1.1 }
          - probe: { quantity: current, on: wire, touching: L1.2 }
  - observe: { run-for: 0.5 s, compare-with: 2 }        # shows step 2's prediction beside the result
  - explain: { prompt: "Why are the two currents equal?", report-text: false }   # XAP-05

A lesson file cannot run code (LES-02). Every field is data from a closed vocabulary of step types and check types; there is no expression language beyond comparison operators and tolerances. The loader validates the schema, then checks the lesson against its circuit (unknown labels, impossible checks) and lists every problem for the author (LES-16).

docs.title: 4.2 The step machine
docs.text:
interface LessonEngine {
  load(lesson: LessonFile, circuit: CircuitDocument): LessonValidation;
  readonly step: { index: number; count: number; status: "active" | "complete" };
  next(): void;
  back(): void;
  resetStep(): void;              // restores the document snapshot taken when the step began (LES-12)
  revealHint(): void;             // LES-10
  showMe(): void;                 // performs the step as a document transaction
  submit(answer: Answer): void;   // predictions, measurements, explanations
}

On entering a step the engine:

  1. snapshots the document (for Reset Step);
  2. computes the step's capability set — including hidden for blind predictions and disabling Run when the step requires a prediction first (LES-03) — and hands it to the shell;
  3. sets spotlights (LES-09);
  4. subscribes the step's checks to the data they need.

docs.title: 4.3 Checks
docs.text:
Each check type in LES-06 compiles to a predicate over a read-only lesson context:

interface LessonContext {
  doc: CircuitDocument;
  compiled: CompiledCircuit;      // nodes and connectivity
  live: LiveValues;               // latest frame
  history: HistoryStore;          // for "within tolerance over a time span"
  measure: MeasurementLibrary;    // for RMS, frequency, and the rest
  analysesRun: AnalysisKind[];
  simTimeRun: number;             // for "has run for at least"
}

Checks are re-evaluated whenever a patch or frame could change their answer, at most ten times a second, so a Do step completes the moment the change is made (LES-08). Targeted feedback (LES-11) is attached either to a check that is true in a wrong state or to a diagnostic by its id (for example, ammeter-in-parallel). Test-bench checks run a truth-table job in the analysis worker (History §5.2).

docs.title: 4.4 Random faults
docs.text: A Troubleshoot step with random faults (LES-07) picks one fault with a generator seeded by the learner's identifier and the lesson id, so the choice is stable for one learner and differs between classmates. The fault is applied as a hidden overlay in the netlist compiler (for example, "treat R2 as open"), not as a change to the document. It therefore cannot be undone, does not appear in the inspector, and is not written to saved files or share links, so the answer cannot leak.

docs.title: 4.5 Predictions and progress
docs.text: Predictions are stored with the step that made them and shown by later Observe steps (LES-04). Sketch predictions are stored in the lane's own units and time scale and drawn as a sketch lane (Rendering §5.6). Progress and predictions are saved to the lessons store after every step (LES-13).

docs.title: 4.6 Author mode
docs.text: Author mode (LES-15, a SHOULD) is deferred to a later design pass. The check vocabulary is designed so that each check type can be generated from a selection ("Check this value" on a selected part), which is what author mode will need.

docs.title: 5.1 Turning reporting on
docs.text:
Reporting is off unless both the embed URL has xapi=1 and the host sends configureXapi (XAP-01). The configuration chooses one of two transports:

Transport How it works Relay (recommended for the book) Statements go to the host page through the bridge; the page's own learning-record-store connection sends them. Credentials never enter the simulator. Direct The simulator posts statements to the named LRS endpoint with the credentials from the configureXapi message. Credentials in the URL are refused (XAP-02).

While reporting is on, the status bar shows "Activity recording on", which explains in plain words what is recorded (XAP-03).

docs.title: 5.2 From actions to statements
docs.text:
The reporter does not watch the user interface. It listens to three streams that already exist:

  • executed commands from the command registry (run, pause, reset, analyses);
  • document patches from the edit system (parts added or removed, values changed, switches flipped, probes placed);
  • lesson events from the lesson engine (predictions, checks, hints, progress, completion).

A mapping table turns each event into a statement with the verb, object, and result data from Section 21.2. A coalescer merges continuous actions (slider drags, repeated running) so that no single continuous action produces more than one statement per second, and a slider drag produces exactly one statement when it ends (XAP-08).

docs.title: 5.3 Identity and identifiers
docs.text:
• The actor comes only from the host's configureXapi; without one, the reporter uses an anonymous random identifier kept in this browser (XAP-04).
  • Activity identifiers are built from the page address (without query or fragment), the embed id, and the circuit or lesson id, so the same activity on the same page always has the same identifier (XAP-07).
  • Free-text answers are included only when the lesson marks them for reporting (XAP-05).

docs.title: 5.4 Never in the way
docs.text: Statements are built and queued in idle time, never on the frame path. Unsent statements wait in the xapiQueue store, are retried with back-off, and are dropped after seven days (XAP-06).

docs.title: 6. Open questions
docs.text:
1. The book's existing xAPI convention. This book's MicroSims already have an "instrumented" status in mkdocs.yml, using a shared lrs-sim.js script and an ?xapi=teaching URL switch. Should the simulator's relay transport and embed.js reuse that script and convention, so that MicroSims and simulator embeds report the same way? This design recommends it, once the two conventions have been compared in detail.
  2. Lesson file location. Should lesson files live beside the chapter that uses them (docs/chapters/…/lessons/) or in one shared folder?

docs.title: Files and Persistence
docs.text: There are no accounts and no server (Section 18). A student's work lives in three places: files they save, links they share, and their own browser storage. This page designs all three, plus the Falstad importer that opens the book's example library.

docs.title: 1. Components
docs.text: Component Responsibility Format codecs (formats package) Pure functions that convert between a CircuitDocument and the native file, a share link, Falstad text, Falstad XML, and Falstad links. No browser APIs, so they run in the Node test suite. File service Opening and saving files with the browser's file APIs, drag-and-drop, and the unsaved-work guard (FIL-04). Persistence service Everything in IndexedDB: My circuits, autosave and recovery, My parts, lesson progress, the xAPI queue (FIL-08, FIL-09, PRF-06). Service worker Offline operation and the cached example library (PRF-07).

docs.title: 2.1 Options considered
docs.text:
FIL-01 asks for a documented, versioned, human-readable text format in which a reader can see each part, its value, and its connections.

Option For Against Verdict JSON with a published JSON Schema Unambiguous; parsed natively and fast; the schema validates files and documents the format at once; the same structure feeds share links Wordier than the alternatives; no comments Chosen YAML Easier to read and edit by hand; allows comments Parsing surprises (implicit typing of values such as no or 1e3); a parser adds roughly 40 kB; files are written by the program, so hand-editing matters less Rejected for circuits; used for lessons, which people do write by hand (Embedding §4.1) A SPICE-like line format Very compact; familiar to engineers Needs its own documented grammar and hand-written parser; awkward for probes, lanes, sliders, and settings Rejected

docs.title: 2.2 Shape of a file
docs.text:
Files use the extension .circuit.json and are pretty-printed with one part per line, so a file opened in a text editor reads like a parts list:

{
  "format": "circuit-simulator",
  "formatVersion": 1,
  "meta": { "title": "RC charging", "description": "Close S1 and watch C1 charge." },
  "settings": { "realisticParts": false, "realisticRatings": false, "start": "zero", "seed": 1 },
  "parts": [
    { "id": "p1", "type": "battery",   "label": "V1", "at": [0, 0],  "rot": 90, "props": { "voltage": 10 } },
    { "id": "p2", "type": "switch",    "label": "S1", "at": [0, -4], "rot": 0,  "props": { "closed": false } },
    { "id": "p3", "type": "resistor",  "label": "R1", "at": [4, -4], "rot": 0,  "props": { "resistance": 10000 } },
    { "id": "p4", "type": "capacitor", "label": "C1", "at": [8, -4], "rot": 90, "props": { "capacitance": 0.0001 } },
    { "id": "p5", "type": "ground",    "label": "",   "at": [0, 4] }
  ],
  "wires": [
    { "id": "w1", "points": [[0, 0], [0, 4]] }
  ],
  "probes": [
    { "id": "r1", "name": "V1", "quantity": "voltage", "target": { "kind": "across", "part": "p4" }, "lane": "l1" }
  ],
  "lanes": [ { "id": "l1", "kind": "analog" } ],
  "view": { "center": [4, 0], "zoom": 1 },
  "netlist": {
    "_note": "Written for readers only and ignored when the file is opened.",
    "V1": ["N1", "GND"], "S1": ["N1", "N2"], "R1": ["N2", "N3"], "C1": ["N3", "GND"]
  }
}

Design notes:

  • Values are numbers in SI base units (0.0001, not "100u"), so a file never depends on a locale or on the number parser.
  • Connections are visible. Geometry is the truth on load, but every save also writes a netlist section that lists each part's nodes. It is regenerated on every save and ignored on load, so it can never disagree with the drawing. It exists so that a person reading the file can see the connections (FIL-01).
  • Identifiers (id) are stable and internal; labels are what the student sees (Circuit Model §2.1).
  • Saved part state (capacitor voltages and the like) is written as savedState on each part, matching Falstad's behavior (FIL-17).

docs.title: 2.3 Versions
docs.text:
Each released change to the format increases formatVersion and ships a migration function from the previous version. Opening a file runs the chain of migrations up to the current version (FIL-03, backward). A file from a newer version is opened as far as possible: unknown part types become placeholders that keep their raw data, so saving again does not lose it, and a notice explains what happened (FIL-03, forward).

The JSON Schema for each version is published with the simulator, next to a readable description of the format.

docs.title: 3. Share links
docs.text:
A share link carries the whole circuit, compressed, with no server storing anything (FIL-05).

Choice Decision Reason Compression deflate-raw through the browser's built-in CompressionStream Better ratio than lz-string and no library to download. (lz-string is still needed, but only for reading Falstad's ctz links.) Encoding base64url Safe in URLs with no escaping Where in the link In the fragment: …/simulator/#c=… The fragment is never sent to the web server, so circuits are not written to server logs and server URL-length limits do not apply. The c query parameter (Section 19.1) is also accepted, for embeds. Size limit Warn above 8,000 characters (FIL-06) Many chat and email tools truncate longer links

Opening a link always opens a copy (FIL-07): the document is loaded into a new My circuits entry, and the link itself is never changed.

docs.title: 4.1 The importer
docs.text:
Falstad text (`$` line + one element per line) ─┐
Falstad XML (`<cir …>`) ────────────────────────┼─> FalstadCircuit ─> mapper ─> CircuitDocument + import report
Falstad link (`ctz`, `cct`, `startCircuit`) ────┘    (neutral, parsed)
  1. Parsers turn each Falstad format into one neutral structure: a settings record, a list of raw elements (type code, the two points Falstad uses to place every element, flags, and parameters), scopes, sliders, hints, and subcircuit models.
  2. The mapper converts each raw element using the falstad section of the matching element descriptor (Circuit Model §5.1), so the knowledge of how to import a part lives with that part. It converts Falstad's two-point placement on a 16-pixel grid into a position, orientation, and length in grid units (FIL-17).
  3. Scopes become probes and lanes showing the same quantities; docked scopes become chart lanes and on-canvas scopes become lanes on the canvas (CHT-35). Sliders become sliders, hints become a line in the description, and the settings line becomes circuit settings (time step, speed, current speed, voltage color range).
  4. Unsupported elements become placeholders with the same terminals, drawn in the warning color, and are listed in an import report (FIL-16).

Exporting to Falstad's format (FIL-20, a MAY) is deferred. Because each descriptor's mapping is written as a two-way table rather than as code, export can be added later without reworking the importer.

docs.title: 4.2 The built-in example library
docs.text:
The 366 examples in the List of Circuits are shipped as static files beside the simulator, with an index generated at build time from src/setuplist.txt in hausen/circuit-simulator, which keeps Falstad's categories (FIL-18). The library browser (FIL-13) and the example parameter (FIL-19) both read that index. Every example's credit to Paul Falstad and its license notice travel with it.

Two automated tests protect the library: every file must open without an error (acceptance test 20), and 20 author-chosen examples must match reference waveforms captured from Falstad's simulator within 1% (acceptance test 21).

docs.title: 5.1 Options considered
docs.text:
Option Verdict localStorage for everything Rejected. About 5 MB per site, strings only, and blocking; thumbnails and many circuits would not fit. IndexedDB Chosen for everything except learner settings. Large quota, structured records, binary thumbnails, transactions. Origin Private File System Rejected for now. Good for large binary files, but our records are many small structured objects, which IndexedDB handles more naturally.

Learner settings stay in localStorage because they are tiny and must be read synchronously before the first frame (Application Shell §8).

docs.title: 5.2 Stores
docs.text: IndexedDB store Key Contents Requirement circuits Circuit id Document, name, thumbnail (PNG), last changed FIL-08 recovery Tab session id The latest document of each open tab, with its file name if any FIL-09, PRF-06 embeds Page address + embed id + hash of the original circuit The reader's changes to an embedded circuit PRF-06 subcircuits Definition id My parts definitions EDT-35 lessons Page address + lesson id Lesson progress and stored predictions LES-13 xapiQueue Sequence number Statements waiting to be sent, with their age XAP-06

docs.title: 5.3 Autosave and recovery
docs.text:
• After each committed transaction, the persistence service writes the document to recovery after a one-second pause, and again at once when the page is hidden. A crash, closed tab, or reload therefore loses at most a second of work (PRF-06).
  • On startup, any recovery entries left by sessions that did not close cleanly are offered back (FIL-09).
  • Several tabs coordinate through a BroadcastChannel, so two tabs never overwrite each other's recovery entry and a circuit open in two tabs is flagged.
  • Embedded circuits are keyed by the hash of the original circuit as well as the page and embed id. If the author later changes the circuit on that page, the reader's old changes are not applied to a different circuit.
  • The first time a student saves to My circuits, the app asks the browser to make storage persistent, so the browser does not evict it under storage pressure, and explains that the list lives only in this browser (FIL-08).

docs.title: 5.4 Opening and saving files
docs.text: Where the File System Access API exists (Chrome and Edge), Save writes back to the same file after the first time. Elsewhere (Firefox and Safari), Save downloads the file. Open uses a file picker everywhere, and dropping a file on the simulator opens it (FIL-04). Every path that replaces the current circuit first checks for unsaved changes and asks.

docs.title: 6. Offline operation
docs.text:
A service worker scoped to the simulator's own folder (so it never affects the rest of the book) caches the application on first visit and the example library in the background afterward (PRF-07).

  • Updates never interrupt work. When a new version is available, the status bar offers "A new version is ready — reload when convenient". The app never reloads itself mid-session.
  • Embeds share the cache, because chapter embeds load the same simulator files from the same origin (Overview §6.1).

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: The example library and the Falstad formats come from Paul Falstad's circuit simulator and its browser port, CircuitJS1, which is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 2 or later. The category list is read from src/setuplist.txt in Rodrigo Hausen's hausen/circuit-simulator fork, which follows Falstad's licensing terms. See the List of Circuits for the full credits.

docs.title: History and Analyses
docs.text: This page covers what happens to results after the engine produces them: how traces are stored, how the student moves back through time, how measurements are computed, and how the analysis views (Section 14) run without disturbing the live simulation.

docs.title: 1. Where each kind of result lives
docs.text:
Data Where Precision How long Probed traces (and math traces) History Store, main thread Times Float64, values Float32 At least 100,000 samples per trace (PRF-04); default 500,000 Full circuit state for scrubbing State ring, live worker (Engine §7.4) Float32 The most recent 20,000 steps (CHT-23) Ghost copies History Store Shared with the trace they copy Up to eight per trace (CHT-17) Event markers History Store event log — As long as the trace history Energy totals (PRB-20) Engine, accumulated each step Float64 Since reset Analysis results Analysis Service results cache Float64 Until the circuit changes, then kept as one ghost (ANL-12)

Single precision is enough for drawing and for every chart measurement at the tolerances in Section 26 (about seven significant digits). The two quantities where rounding would accumulate over many steps — energy totals and running integrals — are computed in double precision.

docs.title: 2. The history store
docs.text:
interface HistoryStore {
  /** Append one frame's samples (called by the Frame Bus). */
  append(frame: Frame): void;

  /** A read-only view of a trace between two times, with its level-of-detail index. */
  view(trace: TraceId, t0: number, t1: number): TraceView;

  /** Keep a copy of the visible or full trace as a ghost (CHT-17). Cheap: shares storage. */
  keepGhost(trace: TraceId, label: MessageRef): GhostId;

  /** Events for markers on the time axis (CHT-24). */
  events(t0: number, t1: number): SimEvent[];

  /** Discard history after a time (Restart from here, CHT-22) or all of it (Reset, SIM-03). */
  truncateAfter(t: number): void;
  clear(): void;
}

docs.title: 2.1 Storage layout
docs.text:
All channels in a run share one time column, because the engine reports every channel at every step. Each column is stored as a list of fixed-size chunks of 4,096 samples. A chunk is mutable only while it is the newest; once full it never changes. That gives three cheap operations:

  • Appending writes into the newest chunk.
  • Ghosts keep references to existing chunks rather than copying them.
  • Dropping old history frees whole chunks from the front.

docs.title: 2.2 The summary pyramid
docs.text:
Alongside each value column, the store keeps a pyramid of block summaries. Every block of 64 samples records its minimum, maximum, sum, and sum of squares; every 64 blocks are summarized again, and so on. The pyramid serves two clients:

  • the Chart Renderer draws each pixel column from the minimum and maximum at the right level, so spikes never disappear and drawing cost depends on chart width, not sample count (Rendering §5.3);
  • the Measurement Library computes minimum, maximum, peak-to-peak, average, and RMS over any span from a handful of summaries plus the raw samples at the two ends, so live measurements on a 500,000-sample trace cost microseconds (CHT-30).

Because time steps vary, sums used for averages are time-weighted (each sample weighted by its step), so an average is a true time average and not biased toward moments where the step was small.

docs.title: 2.3 Memory budget
docs.text: At the default limit of 500,000 samples per trace, 16 probes use about 36 MB (32 MB of values plus 4 MB for the shared time column). When a trace passes its limit, the oldest chunks are dropped but their pyramid summaries are kept, so the chart can still draw the distant past at coarse detail. This is the answer proposed to Rendering open question 1; the author may prefer old history to drop off entirely.

docs.title: 3. Moving through time
docs.text:
Scrubbing (CHT-22) touches every component, so it follows one path:

  1. The student drags the playhead or presses an arrow key. The chart sets ChartModel.playhead = t.
  2. The app sends getStateAt(t) to the live worker. The reply arrives within a frame and is published on the Frame Bus as a historical frame, marked with its time.
  3. Every subscriber treats a historical frame exactly like a live one: wire colors, dots, lamp brightness, charge marks, switch positions, hover cards, pinned meters, and the Loop and Junction tools all show that moment (PRN-04).
  4. If t is older than the state ring, the reply is "not available". The chart still moves its readouts, and the schematic shows "Circuit history not available this far back" (CHT-23).
  5. Run resumes from the latest moment. Restart from here sends restartFrom(t); the worker restores the state at t, and the History Store truncates everything after t.

docs.title: 4.1 The measurement library
docs.text:
Measurements are pure functions over a TraceView and a span, in their own package with no knowledge of the chart. The chart's measurement table, the cursor readouts, the multimeter's AC and DC readings, lesson checks (LES-06), and the parameter sweep's "measurement versus parameter" (ANL-18) all call the same functions.

interface Measurement<R> {
  id: MeasurementId;                      // "rms", "rise-time", "time-constant", ...
  needs: "any" | "periodic" | "step";     // CHT-31
  compute(v: TraceView, span: Span, opts: Options): Result<R>;
}

type Result<R> =
  | { ok: true; value: R; provenance: MessageRef }   // CHT-32: "RMS over 3 whole periods from ..."
  | { ok: false; reason: MessageRef };               // "fewer than two periods visible"
