Group Method Value, minimum, maximum, peak-to-peak, average, RMS, AC RMS, area Summary pyramid (§2.2), time-weighted Frequency, period, duty cycle Rising crossings of the average (or a chosen level), located by linear interpolation between samples; whole periods only Rise time, fall time, overshoot, settling time Find the step's initial and final levels, then the crossing times of the chosen percentages Time constant Least-squares fit of an exponential to the step, reported with its fit quality Phase difference, gain Against a second trace, over whole periods of the first Slope at a cursor (CHT-27) Local derivative from the samples either side Cursor snap points (CHT-26) Peaks, valleys, zero crossings, edges, and the 63.2% point, found by the same crossing and extremum routines

docs.title: 4.2 Math traces
docs.text:
A math trace (CHT-33) is defined by an expression such as V1 − V2 or integral(I1).

  • The expression is parsed by a small, safe parser into a syntax tree. It cannot run code (this matters because math traces travel inside shared files and lesson files).
  • Units are derived by walking the tree with the units package's dimensional algebra, so volts times amps is watts and d/dt of volts is volts per second.
  • Because every channel shares the same time column, evaluation is a straight pass over aligned samples. Derivatives use the variable step; integrals use the trapezoidal rule.
  • Math traces are stored in the History Store like any other trace, so they get the pyramid, ghosts, and measurements for free.

docs.title: 4.3 Tools for the circuit laws
docs.text: The Loop tool (PRB-16), the Junction tool (PRB-18), and the potential profile (PRB-17) request channels for the voltages and currents they need, like probes do, but they do not create traces or lanes. The energy panel (PRB-20) reads per-element energy totals that the engine accumulates in double precision each step, which is the only way to guarantee the 0.1% balance.

docs.title: 5.1 Where analyses run
docs.text: Option Verdict In the live worker, pausing the transient run Rejected. ANL-12 asks the frequency response to redraw within half a second while a slider moves C1, and the live animation must not hitch while it does. In a separate analysis worker Chosen. It loads the same engine code, receives the same netlist, and runs jobs without touching the live simulation. It starts the first time an analysis tab opens and stops after a minute idle. A pool of analysis workers Deferred. Parameter sweeps are naturally parallel, so a pool sized to the processor count could speed them up; it can be added behind the same job interface.

docs.title: 5.2 The job interface
docs.text:
interface AnalysisService {
  submit<J extends AnalysisJob>(job: J): JobHandle<ResultOf<J>>;
}

interface JobHandle<R> {
  progress: Observable<number>;            // 0 to 1, for long sweeps (ANL-20)
  partial: Observable<R>;                  // partial results, kept if cancelled
  result: Promise<R>;
  cancel(): void;
}

type AnalysisJob =
  | { kind: "dc"; netlist: Netlist }                                       // ANL-03
  | { kind: "snapshot"; netlist: Netlist; state: DisplayState }            // ANL-07
  | { kind: "ac"; netlist: Netlist; input: Id; outputs: ChannelSpec[]; freqs: FreqRange }  // ANL-08–13
  | { kind: "phasor"; netlist: Netlist; frequency: number }                // ANL-16
  | { kind: "sweep"; netlist: Netlist; param: ParamRef; values: number[];
      sweep: "transient" | "measurement" | "dc"; outer?: ParamSweep }      // ANL-17–19
  | { kind: "spectrum"; samples: TraceSlice; window: WindowShape }         // ANL-22–25
  | { kind: "thevenin"; netlist: Netlist; a: NodeRef; b: NodeRef; frequency?: number }  // PRB-19
  | { kind: "truthTable"; netlist: Netlist; inputs: Id[]; outputs: Id[] }; // DIG-10, LES-06

Stale jobs are cancelled. When the circuit changes while a frequency response is open, the app cancels the running AC job and submits a new one after a 100 ms pause in edits. The previous result is kept as a ghost (ANL-12).

docs.title: 5.3 How each analysis works
docs.text:
Analysis Method DC operating point The engine's DC routine (Engine §8): capacitors open, inductors shorted, Newton with gmin and source stepping. Returns node and part tables and the power balance. Frequency response Find the DC operating point, ask every element for its small-signal stamps, then solve the complex-valued system once per frequency. The sparsity pattern is analyzed once and reused for all 300 frequencies of the default sweep. Markers (−3 dB points, peak, crossings; ANL-11) are found on the main thread from the result. Impedance The same, with a 1 A test source at the chosen port (ANL-13). Phasors One frequency of the same solve, returned as magnitudes and angles (ANL-16). Parameter sweep For each value, apply the parameter as a setParams override and run the requested routine: a transient run from reset for the chosen duration, a transient run followed by a measurement from the measurement library, or a DC solve. Spectrum Resample the variable-step trace onto a uniform grid by interpolation, apply the window (Hann by default), take a real FFT, and find the fundamental and harmonics for THD (ANL-24). The resolution is reported with the result (ANL-25). Thévenin and Norton Two solves at the chosen pair of nodes: open-circuit voltage, then the impedance seen with independent sources zeroed. Truth table Step a purely digital copy of the selection through every input combination with the event kernel. Also used by lesson test benches.

Every result is shown in the chart renderer with a non-time horizontal axis, which gives every analysis cursors, hover readouts, ghosts, and export (ANL-01).

docs.title: 6. Open questions
docs.text: 1. Sweep cost. A transient-family sweep of 20 values on a large circuit could take many seconds in one worker. Should the first release include the worker pool (§5.1), or is a progress bar enough?

docs.title: Rendering and Animation
docs.text: Everything that moves on screen is drawn by three main-thread components that sit outside the React component tree: the Schematic Renderer, the Current Animator, and the Chart Renderer. They are fed by the Frame Bus (Engine §7) and paced by one shared Render Scheduler.

docs.title: 1. The render scheduler
docs.text:
One requestAnimationFrame loop serves every canvas in a simulator instance, so the schematic and the chart are always drawn from the same frame of data (PRN-04: time is shared).

interface RenderScheduler {
  /** Mark part of the picture as needing a redraw on the next frame. */
  invalidate(what: "grid" | "symbols" | "live" | "dots" | "overlay" | "chart"): void;
  /** True while anything is animating; the loop sleeps when this is false. */
  readonly animating: boolean;
}
  • The loop sleeps when nothing changes. Paused, with no pointer activity and no dots moving, nothing is drawn. This matters for laptops on battery and for pages with several embeds.
  • Off-screen embeds stop drawing. An IntersectionObserver and the page-visibility event stop the loop and tell the worker to pause (EMB-07).
  • Each layer redraws only when invalidated. A switch flip invalidates live and dots; a pan invalidates everything; a hover invalidates overlay only.

docs.title: 2.1 Drawing technology
docs.text: Option For Against Verdict SVG (DOM) Crisp at any zoom; every part is an element, so hit testing and accessibility come cheaply Thousands of moving dots and per-frame color changes mean thousands of DOM updates per frame; falls well short of 30 fps at 150 parts (PRF-01) Rejected for live drawing; used for export Canvas 2D, layered Fast for this scale; full control of drawing order; text and dashed lines are easy; works everywhere We write our own hit testing and accessibility layer Chosen WebGL (or WebGPU) Fastest for very large scenes Text, dashes, and anti-aliased thin lines are hard; much more code; older school laptops have weak drivers Rejected; not needed at 150–500 parts

docs.title: 2.2 Layers
docs.text:
The schematic is drawn on stacked canvases, from back to front, plus one HTML layer on top:

Layer Contents Redrawn when 1. Grid Faint dots (CAN-02), fading below 40% zoom (CAN-06) Pan, zoom, theme 2. Symbols Part symbols, labels, values, annotations, junction dots, crossing hops (CAN-07–13) Document change, pan, zoom, symbol style 3. Live Wire voltage colors, voltage gradients inside parts (ANI-12–13), power glow (ANI-16), lamp and LED glow (ANI-17), capacitor charge marks (ANI-18), switch contacts (ANI-21), logic colors (ANI-22) Every frame while running 4. Dots Current dots, streaks, trickle shimmer, or static arrows (ANI-01–08, ACC-13) Every animation frame while dots move 5. Overlay Selection, focus outline, hover node highlight (CAN-11), probe flags and leaders (PRB-09), tool previews (PRB-04), loop and junction tools (PRB-16, PRB-18), lesson spotlights (LES-09) Interaction, run state 6. HTML Hover cards, pinned meters (CAN-19), in-place value editor (EDT-25), context menus Through React

Symbols are drawn once per part type, orientation, and zoom level into a cached Path2D, so layer 2 is cheap to redraw. Layer 3 is the expensive one; it redraws wires with their colors every frame, which at 150 parts is a few thousand line segments, comfortably inside a frame budget.

docs.title: 2.3 The drawing interface
docs.text:
Element views draw through a small interface, not directly on a canvas:

interface SymbolGraphics {
  moveTo(p: Point): void; lineTo(p: Point): void; arc(...): void;
  stroke(style: StrokeToken): void; fill(style: FillToken): void;
  text(s: string, at: Point, style: TextToken): void;
  image(name: SpriteName, box: Box): void;     // lifelike view (CAN-14)
}

There are two implementations: one that draws to a canvas and one that writes SVG elements. The second gives schematic export as SVG (FIL-11) and printing (FIL-12) from the same code that draws the screen. Styles are theme tokens, never raw colors, so every view follows the light, dark, and high-contrast themes (CAN-15).

docs.title: 2.4 View transform and hit testing
docs.text:
• The view transform maps grid units to screen pixels (zoom 10–800%, CAN-03) and is session state, except that it is saved in the file on save (FIL-02).
  • Hit testing uses a spatial index (a uniform grid hash, rebuilt from the compiled circuit) of every part's hit shape, every wire segment, every probe flag, and every control region. On a coarse pointer, hit shapes and terminals grow to at least 44 px on screen (RSP-13).
  • Labels and live values are placed by trying a few candidate positions around each symbol and taking the first that does not overlap anything already placed. Labels that cannot be placed at a readable size are hidden and shown on hover (RSP-12, ANI-23).

docs.title: 2.5 Lifelike view
docs.text: The lifelike view (CAN-14) is a third symbol style handled by the same ElementView.drawSymbol call with style = "lifelike". It draws sprites (bulbs, batteries, resistors with color bands computed from their value) instead of line art. Wires become curved leads, drawn by smoothing the same polyline. Animation, colors, probes, and hit testing do not change.

docs.title: 3. The current animator
docs.text: The animator owns one number per drawn segment: its phase, measured in units of dot spacing.

docs.title: 3.1 The rule
docs.text:
Each animation frame, for every segment s carrying current I:

phase[s] += speed(I) × Δt_animation / spacing

and dots are drawn at distances (i − frac(phase[s])) × spacing along the segment, for every whole i that falls on it. Because spacing is constant (ANI-04) and speed is proportional to current in the default scale (ANI-03), the number of dots passing any point per second is exactly proportional to the current there. Kirchhoff's current law at a junction (ANI-05) therefore holds by construction, not by tuning.

  • speed(I) is k × I on the proportional scale, or a logarithmic curve on the wide-range scale. The constant k comes from the Current speed control (ANI-10). In Auto, k is chosen so the largest visible current moves four grid units per second, and it is changed only after the largest current has moved by more than ten times for a full second.
  • Δt_animation is real elapsed time while running. It is never scaled by the simulation speed (ANI-03).
  • While paused, stepping, or scrubbing, the phase is moved by the simulated-time change instead, converted at the present speed setting. Stepping forward advances the dots by what that step represents; dragging the playhead back moves them back (ANI-09), so the student can rock the animation around a moment.
  • Direction. Electron flow negates I and swaps the dot sprite (ANI-07).
  • Limits. Below the trickle threshold the dots stay still and shimmer; above the speed cap they are drawn at the cap as short streaks (ANI-06).
  • Reduced motion. When reduced motion is on, the animator draws a static arrow per segment, sized by the current, instead of dots (ACC-13).

docs.title: 3.2 Where the currents come from
docs.text: Every frame carries the latest segment currents: one value per drawn wire segment and per path inside each part, computed by the engine from the solution with each element's segmentCurrents (Engine §5). The compiler's segment table maps them to screen geometry. Currents inside wires are not otherwise known to MNA (a node is one voltage), so the engine finds each wire segment's current by walking the wire tree of each node from its leaves, summing the terminal currents that feed it. This is done once per frame for drawing, not once per step.

docs.title: 4. Voltage color, power, and other live effects
docs.text:
• Voltage color maps each node's voltage through a lookup table for the active scale (red–gray–green, or blue–gray–orange for color-blind safety; ANI-12, ACC-12), one table per theme. The scale range follows the largest voltages present, with the same expand-fast, shrink-slow rule as the chart (ANI-14), unless the student fixes it.
  • Gradients inside parts use the two terminal colors (ANI-13).
  • Power view replaces the table with a warm scale for absorbing parts and a cool one for delivering parts (ANI-16).
  • Flicker suppression (ACC-14). Any element whose drawn brightness or color would change direction more than three times per real second is drawn at its running average instead. The animator tracks this per element with a short history of reversals.
  • Change highlights (ANI-26). After a value change, the renderer compares each node voltage and segment current one simulated second later with its value at the change, and briefly outlines those that moved by more than 10%.

docs.title: 5.1 Build or borrow
docs.text: Option Verdict Plotly or Chart.js Rejected. Large downloads (Plotly especially), and their models (datasets redrawn on update) are not built for 100,000 samples streaming at 60 fps. Lanes with a shared axis, a playhead driving the schematic, ghosts, triggers, and logic lanes would all fight the library. uPlot A strong candidate: small and very fast for time series. Rejected narrowly, because nearly every feature in Section 12 (lanes with two units, trigger modes, a draggable playhead, logic and bus lanes, X-Y view, lanes on the canvas, sketch predictions) would live in plug-ins that work around its model. We borrow its ideas: drawing min/max per pixel column and caching paths. Custom Canvas 2D renderer Chosen. About as much code as uPlot plus the plug-ins, but shaped around this specification. WebGL plot library Rejected: not needed for 16 traces, and weaker text and dashes.

docs.title: 5.2 Structure
docs.text:
Chart panel (React)
  Legend chips, lane titles, menus, measurement table      DOM, for accessibility and drag-and-drop
  Plot area                                                 one canvas per lane, plus one for the time axis
      reads  ChartModel (session state) and Lane[] (document)
      reads  History Store through its level-of-detail index

interface ChartModel {
  window: { start: number; span: number };   // CHT-07
  mode: "roll" | "sweep" | "triggered";      // CHT-08–10
  trigger?: TriggerSpec;                     // trace, level, direction, pre-trigger, auto/normal/single
  live: boolean;                             // false after the student pans back (CHT-21)
  playhead?: number;                         // set when paused (CHT-22)
  cursors?: { a: number; b: number; snap?: SnapMode };   // CHT-26
  hover?: number;                            // CHT-25
}

docs.title: 5.3 Drawing a trace fast
docs.text: The History Store keeps, for each trace, a min/max pyramid: for every block of 64 samples its minimum and maximum, then for every 64 blocks, and so on. To draw a trace across w pixel columns, the renderer picks the coarsest pyramid level that still has at least one entry per column and draws a vertical line from minimum to maximum in each column (CHT-19, PRF-05). Short spikes can never vanish, and drawing cost depends on the width of the chart, not on the number of samples. When zoomed in far enough, it draws the raw samples and marks each one with a dot (CHT-16).

docs.title: 5.4 Sweep and trigger
docs.text: The roll mode simply draws the latest window. Sweep and triggered modes need a sweep start time. A small trigger detector watches the incoming samples of the trigger trace for a level crossing in the chosen direction and records crossing times. In Auto mode it supplies a start time after one window with no trigger; in Single mode it stops after one sweep and sets live = false (CHT-10).

docs.title: 5.5 Vertical scaling
docs.text: Each lane keeps an automatic range that expands at once when a trace leaves it and shrinks only after the traces have used less than a quarter of it for two real seconds, rounded to 1, 2, or 5 times a power of ten (CHT-12). Manual ranges lock the lane until Auto is pressed (CHT-13).

docs.title: 5.6 Other lane kinds
docs.text:
Lane kind Drawing Analog Line per trace, optional second unit axis on the right (CHT-03) Logic Compact high/low line, red band for X, mid-level blue for Z (DIG-07) Bus Labelled value segments in binary, decimal, or hex (DIG-08) X-Y One trace against another, fading trail, bright current point that follows the playhead; optional brightness and color traces for Falstad's 2-D scopes (CHT-34) On canvas Any lane drawn into a box on the schematic's live layer, panning and zooming with it (CHT-35) Sketch A lesson's sketch prediction, drawn with the pointer in the lane's own units and shown dashed beside the real trace (LES-04, LES-05)

All lane kinds share the same axis, cursor, and hover code. The chart in the analysis tabs (frequency, sweep, spectrum) uses the same renderer with a different horizontal axis (frequency or a part value instead of time), which is how every analysis gets cursors, hover readouts, ghosts, and export at once (ANL-01).

docs.title: 6. Open questions
docs.text: 1. Very long runs. The History Store bounds memory (see History §2); the renderer copes with any length. Is it acceptable for the chart to show coarser detail beyond the oldest full-resolution sample, or should old history simply drop off?

docs.title: Simulation Engine
docs.text: The engine turns a netlist into voltages and currents over time. It runs in a web worker (Overview §4), has no access to the page, and talks to the rest of the application only through the worker protocol. Because it depends on nothing but the element models, the units package, and dmath, the same code runs headless in Node for the acceptance tests.

docs.title: 1. Responsibilities and boundaries
docs.text: The engine does The engine does not Solve the circuit at each time step (transient analysis) Know anything about geometry, wires as drawn, or the screen Run the digital event kernel and couple it to the analog solver Decide what a probe looks like or which lane it goes in Choose and adapt the time step (SIM-07, SIM-08) Keep the undo history Find the DC operating point (SIM-12, ANL-03) and run small-signal analyses (in the analysis worker) Format numbers or write messages in English Track heating, ratings, and failure (RLM-04–06) Store probe traces long-term (the History Store does) Keep a ring buffer of full circuit states for scrubbing (CHT-23) Report numerical problems as diagnostics tied to elements (SIM-14, SIM-16)

docs.title: 2.1 Formulation: modified nodal analysis
docs.text:
The engine uses modified nodal analysis (MNA), the formulation used by SPICE and by Falstad's simulator. The unknowns are every node voltage (ground excluded) plus one current for each element that needs one (voltage sources, inductors, ideal op-amp outputs, controlled voltage sources). Each element stamps its contribution into the matrix A and right-hand side b, and the engine solves A x = b.

MNA was chosen without serious competition: it handles every element in Section 9, it is the standard formulation in the literature, and it lets elements be written independently as plug-ins (§5).

docs.title: 2.2 Time integration
docs.text:
Capacitors, inductors, and other elements with memory are replaced at each step by a companion model (a conductance in parallel with a current source) derived from an integration rule. The choice of rule decides whether SIM-22 ("no invented damping") can be met.

Option Behavior Verdict A. Backward Euler, fixed step Very robust; never rings Rejected as the default. It adds numerical damping: an ideal LC circuit loses amplitude every cycle. At 50 steps per period the amplitude falls far below 99% after 100 cycles, failing SIM-22 and acceptance test 6. B. Trapezoidal rule, adaptive step, with backward-Euler restarts Second-order accurate and energy-conserving on ideal LC circuits; can show a small false "ringing" just after a sudden jump Chosen. The ringing is removed the standard way: the first one or two steps after any discontinuity (a switch, a source edge, a digital event) use backward Euler, then trapezoidal resumes. C. Gear's second-order method (BDF2) or TR-BDF2 Never rings; well suited to stiff circuits Rejected as the default. Like backward Euler it damps oscillations slightly, which accumulates over 100 cycles. It remains available as a per-circuit option for very stiff circuits.

docs.title: 2.3 Choosing the time step
docs.text:
SIM-07 asks for the fastest important behavior to span at least 50 steps, with the step shrinking around sudden events. The step is chosen as the smallest of four limits:

  1. Accuracy limit. After each step, each reactive element estimates its local truncation error. If the largest estimate exceeds the tolerance, the step is rejected and retried with a smaller one; otherwise the next step may grow by at most a factor of two.
  2. Time-scale limit. The circuit's fastest time scale divided by 50 (see §2.5).
  3. Breakpoints. The step is shortened to land exactly on the next known event: a source's edge, a scheduled switch action (CTL-08), a digital event, or a chart time the run loop must reach.
  4. Manual limit. The student's maximum time step (SIM-08), when set. If it is larger than the time-scale limit, the engine emits the "step too large" diagnostic.

Crossings that are not known in advance — an analog voltage crossing a logic threshold, a trigger level, a pause condition (SIM-04), a part reaching its failure temperature — are located by checking for a sign change across each accepted step, then shortening the step so it lands within a small tolerance of the crossing.

docs.title: 2.4 Non-linear elements: Newton–Raphson
docs.text:
Diodes, transistors, lamps with realistic filaments, and other non-linear elements are handled by Newton–Raphson iteration at each step. The engine uses the standard aids that make Newton reliable on semiconductor circuits:

  • Voltage limiting on each p-n junction between iterations, so the exponential cannot overflow;
  • a minimum conductance (gmin) across every junction;
  • step halving: if Newton fails to converge in its iteration limit, the step is retried at half the size, up to eight times, before the engine reports SIM-16 ("Could not find a solution at t = …");
  • for the DC operating point, gmin stepping and then source stepping (ramping all sources up from zero) when plain Newton fails.

docs.title: 2.5 Estimating the circuit's time scales
docs.text:
Fit to circuit (SIM-10, CHT-07), the AC slow-down notice (ANI-08), and the time-step limit all need to know how fast the circuit is. The engine computes a TimeScales record whenever the netlist or a value changes:

interface TimeScales {
  fastest: number;      // seconds; drives the step limit
  dominant: number;     // seconds; drives Fit to circuit
  sourcePeriods: number[];   // from every periodic source
  kind: "transient" | "periodic" | "static";
}

Time constants come from the open-circuit time-constant method: for each capacitor (and, dually, each inductor) the engine finds the resistance it sees with every other reactive element frozen, which costs one linear solve per element. The products give a list of time constants; the smallest is fastest, the largest is dominant. Source periods come straight from the source settings. This is approximate for coupled circuits but more than good enough for choosing a speed and a window, and it is cheap enough to recompute on every slider movement.

docs.title: 3. The linear solver
docs.text:
Every step solves at least one linear system. The LinearSolver interface hides how:

interface LinearSolver {
  /** Called when the topology changes: decide the pivot order and fill-in. */
  analyze(pattern: SparsityPattern): void;
  /** Factor the current numeric values. Throws SingularError with the failing row. */
  factor(values: Float64Array): void;
  /** Solve in place using the latest factorization. */
  solve(rhs: Float64Array): void;
}
Option Verdict Dense LU with partial pivoting Used for small systems (fewer than about 40 unknowns), where it is fastest and simplest. Most first-course circuits fall here. Sparse LU with Markowitz ordering (a KLU-style design written in TypeScript) Used for larger systems. The pivot order is worked out once per topology (analyze) and reused for every step, so only the numeric factorization repeats. Iterative solvers (conjugate gradient, GMRES) Rejected. MNA matrices are non-symmetric and often badly conditioned; direct factorization is more reliable and fast enough at this size.

Two further savings matter for smooth animation. If the circuit is linear and the step has not changed, the matrix has not changed either, so the engine reuses the last factorization and only re-solves; most classroom circuits spend nearly all their time in this fast path. And elements mark their matrix entries as static or per-step at setup, so a per-step restamp touches only the entries that change.

Singular matrices become diagnostics, not crashes. When factorization fails at a row, the engine looks up which node or branch current that row belongs to and which elements stamp into it, and reports them (SIM-14). The netlist compiler catches most structural causes earlier (sources in parallel, loops of ideal inductors), so the engine's report is a fallback for the rest.

docs.title: 4. Mixed signal: the digital event kernel
docs.text:
Section 17 asks for a full digital library that mixes freely with analog parts, with four logic states (DIG-02) and propagation delays as short as 10 ns (acceptance test 18).

Option Description Verdict A. Everything analog Each gate is a behavioral voltage source whose output follows a threshold function of its inputs, solved inside the analog matrix (Falstad's approach). Rejected. A 10 ns delay would force 10 ns steps for the whole circuit, even when the digital part is idle; four-state logic (X and Z) has no natural analog meaning. B. Separate event-driven kernel with bridges Digital parts are evaluated by a classic event queue. Bridges convert at the boundaries. Chosen. C. Everything digital, analog parts approximated — Not considered further: the course is mostly analog.

How option B works:

  • The event queue holds pending changes (time, net, newState). Evaluating a gate whose input changed schedules its output change after its propagation delay. Zero-delay gates use delta cycles at the same time, so ordering is still correct and glitches appear when delays are set (DIG-05).
  • Digital-to-analog bridges. Where a digital output drives an analog node, the bridge stamps a voltage source with an output resistance (DIG-04) into the analog matrix. Its voltage changes only when the digital state changes, and each change is a breakpoint for the analog step.
  • Analog-to-digital bridges. Where an analog node drives a digital input, the bridge watches for threshold crossings (with hysteresis for Schmitt inputs) using the crossing detector in §2.3, and posts an event at the crossing time.
  • Synchronization. Each analog step runs to the earliest of its own limit and the next digital event, processes all events at that time, re-stamps changed bridges, and continues. A purely digital circuit advances event to event without solving any matrix at all.

Nets that connect only digital pins never enter the analog matrix. A net with both kinds of pin is an analog node with bridges on it.

docs.title: 5. The element model interface
docs.text:
Every part type in Section 9 is a plug-in with three parts: a descriptor, a model, and a view (Circuit Model §5). The model is the engine's half. It is the only place where a part's physics lives.

interface ElementModel {
  /** Called once per netlist. Declare extra unknowns, matrix entries, digital pins, state size. */
  setup(ctx: SetupContext): void;

  /** Entries that never change while the topology and values are unchanged. */
  stampStatic?(s: Stamper): void;

  /** Entries that depend on the step: companion models, time-varying sources. */
  stampStep?(s: Stamper, step: StepInfo): void;

  /** Linearized entries at the present Newton guess (non-linear elements only). */
  stampNewton?(s: Stamper, x: SolutionView): void;
  hasConverged?(x: SolutionView, previous: SolutionView): boolean;

  /** Called once a step is accepted: update internal state (charge, flux, temperature). */
  accept(x: SolutionView, step: StepInfo): void;

  /** Local truncation error estimate, to choose the next step. */
  truncationError?(step: StepInfo): number;

  /** Known events between t0 and t1 (source edges, scheduled actions). */
  breakpoints?(t0: number, t1: number, out: number[]): void;

  /** Digital behavior: called by the event kernel when an input pin changes. */
  evaluateDigital?(ctx: DigitalContext): void;

  /** Values for hover cards, probes, and Explain (CAN-17, PRB-21). */
  readouts(x: SolutionView, out: ReadoutSink): void;

  /** Current along each drawn segment, for the dots (ANI-01). */
  segmentCurrents(x: SolutionView, out: Float64Array): void;

  /** Heating and rating checks when realistic ratings are on (RLM-05). */
  stress?(x: SolutionView, step: StepInfo): StressReport | undefined;

  /** Serialize and restore internal state, for re-mapping and history. */
  saveState(out: Float64Array): void;
  loadState(from: Float64Array): void;
}

Design notes:

  • Models are written once and used everywhere. Transient, DC, small-signal (AC), and sweep analyses all use the same model. For frequency response the engine asks the model for its small-signal stamps at the operating point through stampStep with a StepInfo.kind of "ac" and a complex frequency.
  • Failure is a model state, not a different element. When stress reports that a part has passed its limit, the model switches into its failure mode (open, short) and the engine emits a partFailed event. The part's identity, label, and probes stay the same (RLM-06). Lamp filament temperature (ANI-17) uses the same heating machinery with ratings turned off.
  • Subcircuits are flattened before they reach the engine, with hierarchical identifiers (U1/R3), so the engine never sees hierarchy. See Circuit Model §6.

docs.title: 6. The engine host and run loop
docs.text: The engine host wraps the engine inside the worker. It owns the run state, turns real time into simulated time, applies commands at safe points between steps, and batches results into frames.

docs.title: 6.1 Run states
docs.text:
load / reset
               |
               v
  +-------> PAUSED <----------- pause / pause condition met
  |          |   ^ \
  |      run |   |  \ step / stepToEvent
  |          v   |   v
  |        RUNNING   STEPPING --(done)--> PAUSED
  |          |
  |   solver error
  |          v
  +--- STOPPED (error) ---- edit makes circuit solvable ---> previous state (SIM-15)

Every circuit loads paused at t = 0 (SIM-01a). Even so, the host computes the solution at t = 0 straight away, so the schematic shows correct wire colors and the hover readouts work before the student presses Run.

docs.title: 6.2 The loop
docs.text:
The worker has no requestAnimationFrame, so the host drives itself with a message-channel tick. Each tick:

  1. Apply pending commands (value changes, switch flips, topology swaps) in the order they arrived. These are the only moments the netlist can change, so a step never sees half an edit.
  2. Compute the budget. Simulated time owed = speed × real time since the last tick, capped so that no more than about 8 ms of computing is spent per tick.
  3. Step the engine until the budget is used, the 8 ms limit is hit, or an event (pause condition, error) stops it.
  4. Emit a frame if at least 16 ms have passed since the last one and the main thread has acknowledged the previous frame.

If step 3 hits the 8 ms limit before the budget is used, the circuit is too slow for the requested speed. The host then lowers the effective speed rather than letting debt pile up, and sets slowerThanRequested in the next frame (PRF-09).

Back-pressure. The host never has more than two unacknowledged frames in flight. If the main thread falls behind (a busy laptop, a background tab), the host merges results into the pending frame instead of posting more, so memory cannot grow without bound.

docs.title: 6.3 Live edits and topology changes
docs.text: Value changes (SIM-18) arrive as setParams and are applied at the next tick; the matrix entries are marked dirty and refactored. Topology changes (SIM-19) arrive as a complete new netlist plus an identity map. The host builds the new engine structures, then copies the saved state of every element whose identifier survived (capacitor voltage, inductor current, flip-flop state, temperature) into its new slot. New elements start from their initial conditions. Then it continues from the same simulated time.

docs.title: 7. The worker protocol
docs.text: All communication with the live worker and the analysis worker goes through typed messages. The protocol is versioned with the application and validated at the boundary in development builds.

docs.title: 7.1 Commands (main thread to worker)
docs.text: Command Payload Requirement load Netlist, circuit settings, initial states FIL-02 replaceNetlist New netlist plus identity map SIM-19 setParams List of (elementId, param, value) SIM-18, CTL-06 setChannels The list of probe channels to record (see §7.3) PRB-01 run, pause — SIM-01 step, stepToEvent — SIM-02 reset Starting mode (zero or steady state) SIM-03, SIM-12 setSpeed Simulated seconds per real second, or "fit" SIM-09, SIM-10 setPauseConditions List of conditions SIM-04 getStateAt A simulated time CHT-22 restartFrom A simulated time CHT-22 setVisibility Visible or hidden EMB-07 ackFrame Frame number Back-pressure (§6.2)

docs.title: 7.2 Messages (worker to main thread)
docs.text: Message Contents frame Simulated time range, the new samples for every channel, the latest display state, run state, effective speed, events since the last frame stateAt The full display state at the requested time, or "not available" (CHT-23) diagnostics The current list of numerical diagnostics (§3, SIM-14, SIM-16) timeScales The latest TimeScales audio Sample blocks for speakers, only when sound is on and running in real time (ANI-20)

docs.title: 7.3 Channels and the frame layout
docs.text:
A channel is one recorded quantity: a node voltage, a voltage between two nodes, a branch or segment current, a power, a logic state. Probes, meters, the Loop and Junction tools, lesson checks, and pause conditions all ask for channels. The main thread deduplicates them, so ten consumers of one node voltage cost one channel.

A frame is packed into a single ArrayBuffer and transferred, not copied:

FrameHeader   frame number, t0, t1, sample count n, channel count k, flags
times         Float64Array[n]          variable-step sample times
samples       Float64Array[n * k]      channel-major
display       Float64Array[nodes + segments]   latest node voltages and segment currents
discrete      Uint8Array[...]          switch positions, logic states, failure flags
events        JSON-encoded tail        switch flips, failures, crossings (CHT-24)

Every step is a sample; nothing is thinned out in the worker, so the History Store can keep full resolution (PRF-04) and measurements are exact. At the time steps typical of classroom circuits this is a few hundred samples per frame.

docs.title: 7.4 The full-state history ring
docs.text:
Scrubbing (CHT-22) needs every node voltage and segment current at any of the last 20,000 steps (CHT-23), not just the probed channels. Sending all of that to the main thread every frame would cost tens of megabytes per second. Instead, the history ring lives in the worker:

Option Verdict A. Ring buffer of display states in the worker, queried with getStateAt Chosen. A scrub costs one small request and reply, well under a frame. B. Ring buffer on the main thread, filled by frames Rejected: the transfer volume described above. C. Periodic checkpoints in the worker, re-simulating forward to the requested time Kept as the fallback for very large circuits (below), since it uses far less memory.

The ring stores the display state as Float32 (single precision is plenty for colors, dots, and hover cards; probed traces keep full precision in the History Store). For a 150-part circuit this is about 20 MB for 20,000 steps. Above a memory budget (default 64 MB), the ring switches to option C: it keeps a full engine checkpoint every 256 steps and re-simulates forward from the nearest one. Determinism (Overview §5.1) makes the replay exact.

A pleasant consequence: when a probe is added while paused, the host can back-fill its trace from the ring, so the new trace shows the last 20,000 steps of history at once instead of starting empty.

docs.title: 8. Starting state and the DC operating point
docs.text:
• Start from zero (SIM-12, the default) sets every capacitor voltage and inductor current to its initial condition (SIM-13), usually zero, and solves the circuit at t = 0 with all sources switched on.
  • Start from steady state runs the DC operating point first (capacitors open, inductors shorted, with the Newton aids in §2.4) and uses it as the initial state.
  • The DC tab (ANL-03) uses the same routine in the analysis worker.

docs.title: 9. Open questions
docs.text:
1. Accuracy tolerances. The default relative and absolute tolerances for the truncation-error check need tuning against acceptance tests 4–9 and against frame-rate targets. A starting point is SPICE's defaults (relative 0.001, absolute 1 µV and 1 pA).
  2. Device models. Which published equations (for example, the Ebers–Moll or Gummel–Poon transistor models, and the Shichman–Hodges MOSFET model) to use for each semiconductor in Section 9.6, and where their default parameters come from, belongs in a later, component-level pass.

docs.title: Learning Graph
docs.text:
The learning graph captures how concepts in Circuit Simulator depend on each other. It is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) — every concept has a path back to one or more foundational concepts that have no prerequisites.

Once the learning-graph-generator skill runs, this section will be populated with:

  • Course Description Assessment — quality review of course-description.md
  • Concept Enumeration — the ~200 concepts the book will cover
  • Concept Taxonomy — concepts grouped into 8–12 categories
  • Graph Quality Analysis — DAG structure, foundational and terminal nodes
  • Taxonomy Distribution — concept count per taxonomy category

Use the book-installer skill (option 23) to add an interactive graph viewer once learning-graph.json exists.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
This book includes 1 interactive MicroSims — self-contained, browser-based visualizations you can explore directly. Click any thumbnail to open the MicroSim.

Circuit Simulator Architecture

docs.title: Circuit Simulator Architecture
docs.text: Run the Circuit Simulator Architecture MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim is the interactive version of the architecture diagram in the Circuit Simulator Design. It shows the twenty components of the simulator, which thread each one runs on, and the data that flows between them.

  • The main thread holds everything the reader sees and touches: the interface, the circuit model, the results and drawing components, and storage and reporting.
  • The worker threads hold the numerical work: the live simulation worker (the engine and its run loop) and the analysis worker, which is started only when an analysis tab is opened.
  • The Element Library straddles the boundary, because each part type's plug-in is split into pieces that load on one thread or the other.
  • Dashed arrows are data that crosses between threads as worker messages.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click any component (or choose it from the Component list) to open an info box with its role, what it owns, what it connects to, and the specification requirements it serves. Its connections are highlighted and labelled; everything else fades.
  2. Use Read about the … to jump to that component's section of the design.
  3. Press Next step to trace one edit through the system: a student dragging a slider that changes a resistor while the circuit runs. Each of the seven steps highlights the components and data flows involved. Back steps backward.
  4. Click empty space or press Esc to close the info box.

docs.title: Iframe Embed Code
docs.text:
You can add this MicroSim to any web page by adding this to your HTML:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/circuit-simulator/sims/simulator-architecture/main.html"
        height="557px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Undergraduate, and contributors to the simulator project

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• What a web browser's main thread and a web worker are
  • The idea of a circuit simulation that steps through time

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Students will be able to explain the role of each major component of the circuit simulator and trace how a single edit moves from the interface, through the circuit model and the simulation worker, and back to the screen.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Click each component in the main thread, then each one in the worker threads. For each, say in one sentence what it owns.
  2. Guided practice (5 min): Step through Trace an edit. Before pressing Next each time, predict which component acts next.
  3. Assessment (5 min): Without the MicroSim, sketch the path of a wiring change instead of a value change. Which step differs? (Answer: in step 3 the Netlist Compiler must recompile and send a new netlist with an identity map, so the engine can carry capacitor charge across.)

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the student name the three kinds of state (document, simulation, session) and which component owns each?
  • Can the student explain why the simulation runs in a worker and not on the main thread?
  • Can the student explain why scrubbing publishes historical frames on the Frame Bus?

docs.title: Source
docs.text: The components, their roles, and the seven-step trace are taken from Circuit Simulator Design §3, specifically the component table in §3.1 and the walk-through in §3.2. Each component's info box summarizes its own design page.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Circuit Simulator Design — the architecture this MicroSim illustrates.
  2. Circuit Simulator Specification — the requirements each component serves.
  3. Using Web Workers — MDN, on running scripts in background threads.

docs.title: Embedding the Simulator
docs.text: Any page in this book can hold a working circuit right next to the text that explains it. You write a short <div>, and the book's helper script (docs/js/circuit-embed.js, loaded on every page) turns it into a sized simulator iframe.

docs.title: Example 1: The Built-In RC Circuit
docs.text:
With no circuit named, the simulator shows its built-in RC charging circuit. This embed uses run mode, so you can run it, flip the switch, change values in the inspector, and add probes, but you cannot add, delete, or rewire parts.

<div class="circuit-embed" data-id="demo-rc" data-mode="run"
     data-title="RC charging circuit"></div>

Like every simulation, it loads paused at t = 0. Press Run to start it. Close the switch S1 and watch the capacitor voltage rise with a time constant of RC = 1 s.

docs.title: Example 2: A Series LRC Circuit From the Example Library
docs.text:
Set data-example to a file name from the example library to load one of Paul Falstad's classic circuits. This one shows only the chart and status bar around the circuit, and is view-only.

<div class="circuit-embed" data-id="demo-lrc" data-example="lrc.txt"
     data-mode="view" data-panels="topbar,chart,status"
     data-title="Series LRC circuit"></div>

Every embed shows Reset to original, which restores the circuit as the page published it, and Open in full simulator, which opens the circuit, with your changes, in a new tab where you can edit everything.

docs.title: Embed Parameters
docs.text:
Each data- attribute becomes a URL parameter of the same name on the simulator iframe. You can also write the iframe yourself, as <iframe class="circuit-sim" src="../../simulator/?example=lrc.txt&mode=run&id=ch3-lrc">; the helper script still sizes it.

Attribute Values Default Effect data-example File name in the example library, such as lrc.txt none Loads a library circuit data-circuit URL of a circuit file (native or Falstad text) none Loads that circuit data-c Native share-link payload none Loads a shared circuit data-ctz Falstad compressed circuit text none Loads a Falstad link's circuit data-mode edit, run, view edit What the reader may do (see below) data-panels Comma list of topbar, palette, inspector, chart, status all the mode allows Shows only these panels data-layout auto, side, stacked, circuit, chart auto Forces an arrangement data-lock Comma list of part labels, or all none Locks those parts against editing data-speed 1 to 100 from the circuit Simulation speed setting data-theme auto, light, dark follows the page Color theme data-id Short name generated Names the embed for messages and xAPI data-xapi 1, 0 0 Allows xAPI reporting once the page configures it data-allow Comma list of origins none Other page origins allowed to send messages data-height Pixels from the simulator Fixes the iframe height data-title Text "Circuit simulation" The iframe's accessible title

The modes:

Mode The reader can edit Do everything the full simulator allows run Run, pause, reset, flip switches, change values of unlocked parts, add probes; not add, delete, or rewire parts view Watch, pause, and step; no changes

Parameters the simulator does not know are ignored, and invalid values fall back to their defaults with a warning (shown as a small ⚠ count in the embed bar). The autorun parameter is read but has no effect: every simulation starts paused. An embed scrolled out of view, or in a hidden tab, stops drawing and pauses its simulation until it comes back.

docs.title: Controlling an Embed From the Page
docs.text:
The helper script exposes CircuitEmbed.get(id) for page scripts. Messages are accepted only from a page with the same origin as the simulator, or from an origin named in data-allow.

const sim = CircuitEmbed.get("demo-rc");
sim.setSwitch("S1", true);
sim.setValue("R1", "resistance", 4700);
sim.run();
sim.getState().then((state) => console.log(state.probes));
sim.on("runStateChanged", (p) => console.log(p.runState));
Page to simulator Payload run, pause, step none reset { original: true } restores the published circuit setValue { part, prop, value } (part by label or id) setSwitch { part, closed } addProbe { part } adds a voltage probe across it loadCircuit { example }, { url }, { c }, or { text, name } configureXapi { transport: "relay" } or { transport: "direct", endpoint, auth }, optional actor getState none; replies with the circuit, run state, time, and probe values Simulator to page Payload ready mode, edit level, panels preferredHeight { height }; the helper resizes the iframe runStateChanged { runState } circuitChanged { source, changes } xapiStatement { statement }, also dispatched as a circuit-embed:xapi DOM event reply { ok, result } or { ok: false, error } for requests

Every message uses the envelope { protocol: "circuit-simulator", version: 1, embedId, type, requestId?, payload }. The full design is in Embedding, Lessons, and xAPI.

docs.title: Recording Learning Activity
docs.text: xAPI reporting is off unless the embed has data-xapi="1" and the page sends configureXapi. With the relay transport, each statement comes back to the page as a circuit-embed:xapi event, so the page's own learning record store connection can forward it; credentials never enter the simulator. While reporting is on, the embed shows an Activity recording on indicator that explains what is recorded.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: The series LRC example, lrc.txt, is one of the example circuits from Paul Falstad's CircuitJS1 simulator, from the folder src/com/lushprojects/circuitjs1/public/circuits/. The book's build downloads that folder unchanged into the simulator's example library and opens the file through the simulator's Falstad importer. The example circuits are by Paul Falstad and are used under the CircuitJS1 license; see also Falstad's licensing terms. The built-in RC circuit and the simulator itself are part of this book.

docs.title: Guided Simulator Lessons
docs.text: A lesson turns a circuit into a short guided activity. The learner reads a step, commits to a prediction, changes the circuit, runs it, and types what the meters show. A panel beside the schematic shows Step n of N, enables Next only when the step is done, and offers hints and a Reset step button that puts the circuit back the way the step found it.

docs.title: Try It: Ohm's Law
docs.text:
This lesson asks you to measure the current through a 1 kΩ resistor at three voltages and to predict the current before you measure it. Your progress is saved in this browser, so you can leave and come back.

<div class="circuit-embed" data-id="lesson-ohms-law"
     data-lesson="ohms-law.yaml" data-height="640"></div>

A second lesson, rc-charging.yaml, asks you to predict the capacitor voltage after one time constant, then pauses the simulation at t = τ so you can check the 63% rule. Open either lesson full-size with simulator/?lesson=ohms-law or simulator/?lesson=rc-charging.

docs.title: The Lesson File
docs.text:
A lesson is one YAML file. It cannot run code: every field comes from the fixed vocabulary below, and the simulator checks the file when it loads and lists any problem with its line number. Here is a shortened version of the Ohm's law lesson:

lesson: ohms-law                    # kebab-case id, used for saved progress
title: Ohm's law
time: 10 min
objectives: [Measure the current through a resistor]
concepts: [Ohm's Law, Electric Current]   # names from the learning graph
circuit: circuits/ohms-law.circuit.json   # relative to the lesson file

permissions:
  edit: values                      # full, values, or none
  palette: []                       # part types offered; [] hides the palette
  tools: [select]
  locked: [R1, A1]                  # labels the learner cannot change

steps:
  - read: |
      A DC source **V1** pushes current through R1. Ohm's law: `I = V / R`.
    spotlight: [R1, A1]

  - id: predict-10v
    predict-number:
      prompt: If you double V1 to 10 V, what current will A1 read?
      unit: A
      blind: [readouts, traces]     # hide values until the prediction is in

  - do:
      prompt: Set V1 to 10 V in the Inspector.
      check:
        property: { part: V1, prop: voltage, equals: 10 V, tolerance: 1% }
    hints: [Click V1, then type 10 into its Voltage field.]

  - observe:
      prompt: Press Run and compare.
      run-for: 0.2 s
      compare-with: predict-10v     # shows the prediction beside the result
      show: { part: A1, quantity: current }

  - measure:
      prompt: Type the current A1 reads.
      value: { part: A1, quantity: current }
      tolerance: 2%

The full lessons are in the repository at app/public/lessons/, and the JSON Schema that editors use for autocompletion is lesson-v1.schema.json. Add this first line to a lesson file to get autocompletion in VS Code:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmccreary/circuit-simulator/main/app/packages/lesson/src/schema/lesson-v1.schema.json

docs.title: Step Types
docs.text:
Each step has exactly one type key. Step text is Markdown-lite: paragraphs, **bold**, *italic*, `code`, and bulleted or numbered lists.

Step What the learner does When it is complete read Reads the text At once; Next is enabled predict-number Types a value with units, such as 2.5 mA When a value is submitted predict-choice Picks one of the options When a choice is submitted do Changes the circuit The moment its check passes observe Runs the circuit for run-for simulated seconds When that time has run; the simulation pauses measure Types a reading When it is within tolerance of the true value explain Writes a sentence or picks one of the options When an answer is submitted troubleshoot Selects the faulty part When the right part is chosen

Every step can also carry:

  • spotlight: part labels to outline on the schematic, or controls such as command:sim.runPause and palette:resistor
  • hints: up to three, revealed one at a time; hint use is recorded
  • feedback: messages shown while a wrong state lasts, attached to a simulator warning (diagnostic: ammeter-in-parallel) or to a check (when: { sim-time: 1.2 s })
  • permissions: changes to the lesson's permissions for this step only
  • success: the confirmation shown when the step completes

A troubleshoot step lists possible faults, such as "R2 open", "C1 short", or { part: R1, kind: value, props: { resistance: 100k } }. Each learner gets one fault, chosen by a generator seeded from the learner and the lesson, so classmates usually get different faults. The fault is hidden from the inspector, saved files, and share links.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
A do step's check (and a feedback item's when) is one of these, and checks combine with all, any, and not:

Check Example part part: { type: ammeter, label: A1 }, or exists: false property property: { part: R1, prop: resistance, equals: 2.2k, tolerance: 5% } switch switch: { part: S1, closed: true } connected connected: { a: R1.2, b: GND } (terminal numbers start at 1) probe probe: { quantity: current, part: R1 } value value: { of: { part: C1, quantity: voltage }, equals: 6.32 V, tolerance: 4% } measurement measurement: { probe: V(C1), kind: rms, over: 1 s, above: 3 } diagnostic diagnostic: { id: no-ground, present: false } sim-time sim-time: 1 s run-state run-state: running

Comparisons accept equals with a tolerance (absolute such as 0.05 V, or relative such as 2%), above, below, and within: [min, max]. Part voltages and currents are magnitudes, so a check does not depend on which way a part was drawn. Checks are re-evaluated only when the circuit changes or a new frame of results arrives, at most ten times a second.

docs.title: Progress and Reporting
docs.text:
Progress, predictions, and hints are saved in the browser after every step and restored when the learner returns to the same page. The last step shows a summary of steps completed, predictions next to results, and hints used. When the page enables xAPI, the simulator reports attempted, answered, progressed, and completed statements, and the page receives a lessonProgress message after every step:

CircuitEmbed.get("lesson-ohms-law").on("lessonProgress", (p) => {
  console.log(`step ${p.step} of ${p.of}: ${p.status}`);
});

docs.title: Writing a Lesson
docs.text:
1. Build the circuit in the simulator and save it as a .circuit.json file next to the lesson file.
  2. Open the lesson with ?lesson= and expand Author tools in the lesson panel. Any problems in the file are listed there with line numbers.
  3. Set up the circuit the way a step should end, select the parts that matter, and press Copy step snapshot as YAML. Paste the copied do step into the lesson and delete the checks you do not need.

The design behind this page is in Embedding, Lessons, and xAPI, and the requirements are in Section 20 of the specification.

docs.title: Circuit Simulator Specification
docs.text:
Status Draft 1 for author review Date 2026-10-21 Audience of this document The book author, designers, developers, testers, and lesson writers Primary learners High school physics students and first-year college circuits students

This document specifies, in detail, what a new browser-based circuit simulator must do and how it must behave for the person using it. It does not say how the program should be written. The only technical assumptions are that it runs in a modern web browser and that the person using it has a mouse and a keyboard. Every screen must also be responsive, adapting to any window size from a wide desktop monitor down to a phone.

The specification draws on a feature-by-feature study of Paul Falstad's circuit simulator and a survey of other educational and professional simulators. Those sources are listed in Sources at the end. The book's List of Circuits is the library of example circuits the new simulator must be able to open.

docs.title: 1.1 Requirement language
docs.text:
The words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, and MAY are used as defined in RFC 2119:

  • MUST and MUST NOT are absolute requirements. A build that fails one is not complete.
  • SHOULD and SHOULD NOT are strong recommendations. Leaving one out needs a written reason.
  • MAY marks an optional feature that is welcome but not required for a first release.

docs.title: 1.2 Requirement identifiers
docs.text:
Every requirement has a short identifier, such as PRB-04, so testers, lesson writers, and the user stories in Section 25 can refer to it. The prefix names the section:

Prefix Section PRN Design principles LAY Screen layout RSP Responsive behavior CAN Schematic canvas EDT Building and editing circuits CMP Component library SIM Simulation behavior ANI Current animation and visual feedback PRB Probes and measurement tools CHT The time-series chart ANL Analysis views CTL Interactive controls while running RLM Realism, ratings, and failures DIG Digital logic and mixed signal FIL Files, sharing, and Falstad compatibility EMB Embedding in textbook pages LES Guided lesson mode XAP xAPI learning events ACC Accessibility PRF Performance and reliability SET Settings

docs.title: 1.3 Decisions already made
docs.text:
The book author settled these scope questions before this draft was written. The rest of the document follows them:

Question Decision Primary learners High school physics and first-year college circuits Analyses beyond the live chart DC operating point table, frequency response (Bode plot), parameter sweep, and spectrum (FFT) Digital logic Full analog and digital library, so mixed-signal circuits work Textbook integration Open Falstad circuit files, embed in textbook pages, guided lesson mode, and xAPI learning events Current animation convention Conventional current by default, with electron flow as an option Ratings and failures Ideal parts by default; parts can fail only when a "realistic ratings" option is on Saving and sharing No accounts: files, shareable links, and browser storage only Screen sizes Every user interface surface must be responsive

docs.title: 2.1 Purpose
docs.text:
The simulator exists to help students see what happens inside a circuit. Textbook diagrams are frozen. Lab equipment shows one number at a time. A good simulator shows every wire's voltage, every branch's current, and how both change over time, all at once and in step with each other.

The core experience has three parts that are always visible together:

  1. An animated schematic on the left. Moving dots show current flowing in every wire and through every component, and the color of each wire shows its voltage.
  2. A live time-series chart on the right. Time runs along the x-axis, and the chart plots the voltages and currents the student has chosen to watch.
  3. Probe tools that connect the two. The student drops a voltage probe on a wire or a current probe on a component, and a matching trace appears on the chart at once, in the same color as the probe's flag.

docs.title: 2.2 Goals
docs.text:
• G1 — Insight first. Every feature is judged by whether it helps a student build a correct mental model of how circuits behave.
  • G2 — Two clicks to any waveform. Any voltage or current in the circuit can be on the chart within two clicks of deciding to look.
  • G3 — Predict, observe, explain. The tool supports the learning cycle of making a prediction, testing it, and explaining the difference.
  • G4 — Faithful enough. Results match textbook theory closely for the circuits in the course (see Section 26), while staying fast enough to animate smoothly.
  • G5 — Works in the textbook. Simulations embed in MkDocs pages, open the existing Falstad example library, run guided lessons, and report learning events.
  • G6 — Works everywhere. Any modern browser, any window size, no installation, no account.

docs.title: 2.3 Misconceptions the simulator must address
docs.text:
Physics education research has catalogued the wrong ideas students most often hold about circuits. The simulator's features are chosen to confront each one with something the student can see. Research also warns that animation alone does not fix misconceptions: in one controlled study, students learned equally well with and without the moving-electron display (Keller and others, 2006). What helps is animation combined with a prediction the student has committed to, which is why lesson mode hides the animation until a prediction is made (LES-03).

Misconception What the simulator shows instead Main features Current is used up by each bulb Probes before and after every part read the same current; dots move at one speed all around a series loop; a separate power view shows what is used: energy PRB-01, ANI-03, ANI-16, story 25.1 A battery always delivers the same current The battery's current trace jumps when a parallel load is added while its voltage stays put CHT-17, story 25.2 Sequential reasoning: a change only affects parts "downstream" Every part's current starts and changes in the same instant; all meters and traces move together ANI-02, PRN-02 Local reasoning: current always splits equally at a junction Branch dot speeds and the Junction tool show unequal splits that depend on the whole circuit ANI-05, PRB-18 Voltage is a property of current, or exists only where current flows Wire colors show potential everywhere, including across an open switch carrying no current; voltage probes always measure between two points ANI-12, PRB-01 "The voltage at a point" without a reference Ground is marked; differential probes are drawn with red and black leads CAN-12, PRB-01 Brightness depends on current alone Brightness follows power; power probes and the Power view ANI-17, ANI-16 Current flows through a capacitor's insulator Charge builds up on the plates while the current trace decays ANI-18, story 25.3 Misreading graphs: confusing slope with height Cursor readouts give both the value and the slope; derivative math traces CHT-26, CHT-33 Meters can go anywhere Realistic meters that load the circuit, warnings for wrongly placed meters, a fuse that blows PRB-22, PRB-23, PRB-24, EDT-39

docs.title: 2.4 What changes from Falstad's simulator
docs.text:
Falstad's simulator is the starting point and the source of the example library. This specification keeps its strengths (it is always live, it animates current, it colors wires by voltage) and changes the things that get in a student's way. The left column describes Falstad's simulator as of October 2026 (Sources).

Falstad's simulator today This specification Charts sit in a strip below the circuit, 20% of its height by default Circuit on the left, chart on the right, 60/40, adjustable, responsive (Section 4) Each chart keeps one screen of history, as per-pixel minimum and maximum; changing the time scale erases it Full-resolution history that can be scrolled, zoomed, and scrubbed, with the schematic replaying the past (CHT-22) Charting a voltage between two nodes takes about six actions, and the meter used loads the circuit with 10 MΩ Two actions, with an ideal probe (PRB-01) Charts have no legend; colors are fixed; readouts and the trigger use only the first plot A legend matched to probe flags, chosen colors, and measurements on every trace (CHT-05, CHT-30) Signs follow the direction each part was drawn, shown only while highlighted Every probe shows its sign convention; every part marks its reference terminal (PRB-06, CMP-05) Errors are one line of text, such as "Singular matrix!", often with no part highlighted A plain-language explanation, the parts highlighted, a suggested fix, and automatic resume (SIM-14) Mistyped values are silently ignored; unit symbols are rejected Units accepted, mistakes explained (EDT-26) Undo resets the simulation Undo applies to the running circuit (EDT-33) No visible grid; no voltage color legend Grid and legend (CAN-02, ANI-14) Transient analysis and a DC operating point only Adds DC tables, frequency response, sweeps, and a windowed spectrum (Section 14) Described by its users as unusable on phones and tablets; no keyboard navigation of the circuit Responsive at every size, keyboard-operable, screen-reader friendly (Section 5, Section 22) Speed control has no units; the real-time ratio is hidden below 0.1× Speed stated in words, with Fit to circuit (SIM-09)

docs.title: 2.5 Out of scope
docs.text:
• How the program is written: languages, frameworks, numerical methods, and internal data structures.
  • Printed-circuit-board layout, part ordering, and bills of materials.
  • Sign-off-grade accuracy for professional design. The simulator is a learning tool, not a replacement for SPICE in industry.
  • Electromagnetic field simulation, antennas, and radio-frequency layout effects beyond the transmission-line elements listed in Section 9.
  • User accounts, cloud storage, and class rosters.
  • Microcontroller code emulation (for example, running Arduino programs). This is a possible future extension; see Section 27.

docs.title: 3. Design Principles
docs.text:
• PRN-01 — Show, then tell. The simulator MUST make behavior visible (motion, color, brightness, waveforms) before asking the student to read numbers. Numbers MUST always be one hover or one click away.
  • PRN-02 — Everything is live. While the simulation runs, every edit (changing a value, flipping a switch, adding a probe, even adding or deleting a part) MUST take effect without a separate "run" step.
  • PRN-03 — One color per signal. A probe, its flag on the schematic, its trace on the chart, its row in the legend, and its readouts MUST all share one color, so the eye can match them instantly.
  • PRN-04 — Time is shared. The schematic and the chart MUST always describe the same moment. When the student pauses and scrubs back in time on the chart, the schematic MUST show the circuit as it was at that moment.
  • PRN-05 — Forgiving editing. Every action MUST be undoable. The simulator MUST never discard work without asking.
  • PRN-06 — Helpful errors. When a circuit cannot be simulated (for example, two ideal voltage sources in parallel), the simulator MUST say why in plain language, highlight the parts involved, and suggest a fix.
  • PRN-07 — Ideal by default, real on request. Parts behave ideally unless the student turns on realistic ratings. The student MUST always be able to tell which mode is active.
  • PRN-08 — Progressive disclosure. A beginner sees a short palette of common parts and simple controls. Advanced parts, options, and analyses are one step away and never in the way.
  • PRN-09 — Same circuit, same result. Running the same circuit with the same inputs MUST give the same results every time (including random noise sources, which use a stored seed).
  • PRN-10 — No dead ends on any screen. At every window size every feature MUST remain reachable (see Section 5).
  • PRN-11 — No artificial limits. There MUST be no cap on the number of parts in a circuit, the number of circuits a student keeps, or the features available. (Several commercial tools cap free circuits at five to 25 parts.)
  • PRN-12 — Open and durable. Circuits MUST be saved in an open, documented format, and the simulator MUST keep working offline, so students' work survives even if a hosting service closes. (Multisim Live closed on 2026-09-15 without guaranteeing access to saved designs.)
  • PRN-13 — Prediction before animation. The animation is a means, not an end. The design MUST make it easy to hide the answer and ask for a prediction first (Section 2.3).

The main window has seven regions. The wireframe shows the wide layout:
